speechtext:
GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 197) to amend the Railway Act. He said: This Bill is somewhat lengthy, and I shall briefly refer to the changes it is intended to make in .the existing Act. In the first clause it is proposed to apply the Act so as to require telegraph, telephone, and express, companies to make yearly statements of their business as do the railway companies now. The next paragraph refers to the protection of forests from fire caused by a railway company, and it has been the subject of resolutions by the Conservation Commission, and by the Forestry Association of the Dominion. It was first suggested that the law be made specific and stringent as to what the company should do, but at a meeting between the Chairman of the Conservation Commission, a representative of the western farmers, a member of the Forestry Association, and the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, this clause was decided upon as meeting all requirements'. It makes clear that the Mr. HAGGART (Winnipeg).
Board of Railway Commissioners can compel a railway company to provide facilities for the protection of property contiguous to a railway, to say how many patrolmen should be necessary, what fences should be provided, and to make general rules in this respect. The next clause is to make applicable to telephone, telegraph, and express companies the existing law with reference to railways which names an agent in any locality upon whom notice can be served. The next clause makes clear certain matters as to the location of railways, and that I shall explain on the second reading. The next clause is to provide that lands even though they belong to a railway company and are not for strictly railway purposes, can be treated like lands belonging to any other individual in the matter of expropriation for, say, another railway. The next clause is introduced by arrangement with the Chairman of the Ontario Railway and Municipal Board, and it makes provision by which a joint board can be formed of a member of any provincial board having jurisdiction over these matters, and a member of the Dominion Board of Railway Commissioners, to compel connection to be made between a provincial road and a federal road, and to make provisions for the interchange of traffic.
Will that be in harmony with the statute recently passed by the Ontario legislature?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, but it will apply to any other province having a provincial board organized for similar purposes. The next clause provides for the appraisement of damages to land adjoining or abutting on a highway where the railway has been allowed to run on a highway. There is not in the present law any provision by which the owner of the adjoining property can get damages on account of the railway getting on the highway in front of his property. The next clause is to allow, under general regulations and rules of the Board of Railway Commissioners, wires to cross railways where the railway consents and where the regulations are complied with. At present application has to be made to the board in each case. The next clause is a similar clause with reference to sewers under railways where the railway consents. The next clause has reference to fencing 'along lines of railway under construction. Under the existing Act the railways do not have to fence unless ordered by the board, and the amendment will be somewhat drastic, and will compel the railways to fence unless excused by the order of the board. It places the onus on thfe railway companies to prove

that it is not necessary for them to fence. It also compels the railway company to fence right of way or take other effectual means, such as cattle-guards to prevent cattle getting on the railway. The next section repeals that clause of the Act which prohibits stock from running within half a mile of a railway. There will be some discussion as to the propriety of this in the older parts of Canada, but on the whole it has seemed to those who have considered it, that it is a wise provision in the interest of the western part of Canada where they have the right to graze on these lands that are not inclosed, and under the present Act it is impossible for them, in many cases, to get redress if their stock is killed. In the older provinces-I can speak more particularly of Ontario-most municipalities, by by-law,
_ forbid cattle running at large on the highways, and they may continue to regulate that matter by by-law if they choose to do so.
Will the railways be bound to observe those by-laws?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The by-law does not affect the railway; it affects the man who owns the cattle. But I presume that if a cow were on a highway contrary to a by-law of a municipality, it would be there contrary to law, and that would be a factor in deciding the liability of the railway. The next clause, 12, is merely to make clear a section that was passed last year. Section 13 is one giving the Board of Railway Commissioners powers, in addition to the power given to them by the Act as it now stands, to regulate the price of electric power under their jurisdiction. Further, if a person makes application to a company under the control of the board for a certain quantity of power, and the company declines to give it to him, he can appeal to the board for an order on the company to give the power asked for. Section 14 is in reference to returns to the department as to accidents. The statute says that they shall be made semi-annually. They have been made annually, and we are making it clear that an annual return in general terms is all that is required; but I w'ill introduce a clause into the Bill providing that the minister may ask for a return whenever he sees fit. This is to cover two points: first, if a question arises as to an accident in which lives have been lost, in addition to the particulars required by the Board of Railway Commissioners, the minister may deem it wise in the public interest to ask for further particulars. Power is also given to the minister, where complaint is made that a large quantity of stock has been killed, to require a return to be made more frequently than twelve months, so that
the matter can be investigated. Complaints have been made by farmers in the west that where stock has been killed, the railway company or some person has frequently buried the carcases, and it has sometimes taken a year or two for the owners to find out where the animals have gone, as no trace is left of them. This clause is desired to enable the department to get the proof of the killing of those animals if it is thought to be in the public interest, as often as may be required. Then we propose to add a section to the Act which is quite drastic and may cause some discussion. The main features of it are that where a railway company has been granted a charter by the parliament of Canada, or where a railway has passed into the ownership of a company holding a charter from the Dominion of Canada, if the line is allowed to become dilapidated to such an extent that it is unsafe to operate, the government may step in and declare that the subsidy granted to the railway company shall become a lien upon it to such an extent that the railway can be sold under it. This power may, perhaps, never, at all events not very often, be exercised; but something is necessary to give the department power to compel railway companies or companies owning railways to keep their line in a fit condition to operate. I beg leave to move the first reading of the Bill.

Has the minister dealt, in the Bill, with the question of commutation tickets, so as to prevent railway companies from discriminating in regard to them? I understood that the minister had some sympathy with the municipalities that made their wishes known in that respect, both in the press and by interviewing the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There is nothing in this Bill in reference to commutation tickets.

Does the section in regard to railways which are allowed to fall into disrepair apply to grants made by the Dominion of Canada in the future or to grants made in the past? In other words, will it be retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is debatable, as the Bill is drawn.

Will the joint board have power to deal with electric roads incorporated by the province of Ontario as well as with electric roads and steam railways incorporated by the Dominion? I think the minister knows the case I refer to-the Hamilton case.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Bill gives powrnr to the board to deal with provincial roads as well as Dominion roads.
No matter whether electric or steam?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There is no distinction as to the kind of propelling power.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: Mr. OLIVER moved third reading of Bill (No. 177) to amend the Indian Act.

My contention, when this Bill was brought in, was that the matter should previously go to parliament-that is after the investigations had been made, and before any action was taken regarding this reserve. I see that an amendment has been inserted embodying that idea so that on that point I have no lurther objection.

The hon. minister was good enough the other evening to say that he would consider an amendment I suggested to provide for representation before the courts of such Indians as may be opposed to removal from their reserve. I think the object wmuld be obtained by adding to subsection 3 of section 49A the following words:
And shall assign counsel to represent and act for the Indians who imay ibe opposed to the proposed removal.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The section as it stands, it seems to me, would permit the judge to take the action my hon. friend suggests, but he desires to make that mandatory.

That is one purpose. No doubt the section dealing with the powers of the judge is very large, and it might be contended that under it he will have the power to assign counsel for these Indians. The section reads:
3. The judge shall have the like powers to issue subpoenas, compel the attendance and examination of witnesses, take evidence, give directions, and generally ito hear and determine the matter and regulate the procedure as in proceedings upon information by the Mr. GRAHAM.
Attorney General within the ordinary jurisdiction of the court.
I am not prepared to say offhand whether in any proceeding upon information by the Attorney General, the Exchequer Court has the power to assign counsel to act for parties who are not represented by counsel. If there be a special provision to that effect, my amendment would not he necessary; but if not, I do not think that subsection 3 of section 49A would empower the judge to assign counsel to these Indians. It must be remembered that legally the Indians are represented by the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs; but where there is collision between him and the Indians, the Indians ought to be represented by an independent counsel. The machinery of this Bill will never be set in operation except when the Superintendent General and the majority of the Indians differ in opinion, and in such a case the Indians ought to have a special representative. We should not only give the judge the power to permit such representation, hut we ought to make it his duty to appoint counsel for the Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am quite ready to accept this proposed amendment. I only wish to say that, as I understand the wording of the subsection, adequate provision is made for the appointment of counsel, and as a matter of public policy of course counsel would be appointed. I am quite willing, however, to accept my hon. friend's amendment so that it shall be mandatory on the judge to appoint counsel under certain circumstances. I beg therefore, to withdraw the motion for a third reading .
Motion for third reading withdrawn.
Mr. OLIVER moved that the Bill be referred back to the Committee of the Whole with instructions to amend subsections 3 of section 49A by adding thereto the follow'-ing words:
Ancl shall assign counsel to represent and aot for the Indians who may he opposed to the proposed removal.

While I agree in the amendment suggested by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty), I cannot but think that the Indians ought to have something to say in the choosing of counsel. In this Bill the Superintendent General takes power to himself which the department has never had, and which no Superintendent General has ever had. He is taking the power to take away from the Indians their reserves, and thus violating every treaty made with the Indians without giving them the opportunity to protest in any way against it. The amendment moved provides that the judge may assign counsel. In my opinion the counsel ought to be assigned on the recommendation of the band.

The band ought to have something to say as to who shall represent them. The experience I have had with regard to one of the reserves proves to me that it is quite possible a counsel might be chosen to take the Indians part, who may not have the best interests of the Indians at heart. I think that there ought to be some provision made that the Indians may have something to say in the choosing of their own counsel.
There is another phase of the Bill about which I wish to say a word. The first section of this Bill is to amend section 46 of the Indian Act. Now, section 46 reads as follows:
No portion of any reserve shall be taken for the purposes of any Tailway, road or public work without the consent of the Governor in Council, and, if any railway, road or public work passes through or causes injury to any reserve, or, if any act occasioning damage to any reserve is done under the authority of an Act of parliament or of the legislature of. any province, compensation shall be made therefor to the Indians of the hand in the same manner as is provided with respect to the lands or rights of other persons.
I contend that this clause is contradictory. It starts out first by declaring that no portion of the reserve shall be taken for the purposes of any railway, and then it goes on to provide that if any railway, road or public work passes through and injures the reserve, the parties responsible sfhall be liable for damages. I believe that this part of this section should be rescinded. The amendment proposed by this Bill covers practically everything that is necessary. The change would make the Bill more logical and more easily understood.
As to the Bill as a whole, I desire again to enter my (protest against the principle. The Indians are not represented in this House and have no voice in making this legislation. As I said a moment ago, the minister is asking for power greater than any Superintendent General before ever pretended to ask for. And, in view of the surrender of the St. Peter's Indian reserve. of which I know something, I cannot hope that the Department of Indian Affairs will administer this proposed new law in a manner to commend itself to the sense , of justice of this country. I have no hesitation in saying that under section 49 of the Act, the Indian had some protection, as it remained for the Indian to say. whether he was willing to surrender his reserve or not. And while I believe that the Act has been openlv violated in connection with the surrender of the St. Peter's Indian reserve, yet the Indian has some redress. But, under the proposition before us, he has no redress; it will not be necessary to consult him in connection
with tlhe surrender. When these treaties were made, in most cases the Indians were a power in this country. The treaties had to be lived up to; the Indians were, in many cases, able to compel the white man to keep faith with them. To-day the. Indian is weak. The guardian of the Indian, the Superintendent General, is all powerful in this House. This fact is all the greater reason wlhy the parliament should guard carefully and sacredly the interest of the Indian, the wards of the Canadian people. I contend that the power that the Superintendent General is asking for under this Bill is altogether too 'broad and arbitrary. He is simply taking the power to dispose of people's property and rights without giving them an opportunity i* refuse or to lay their views fairly before the court, or even to a protest against the proceeding. In this country, especially in the province of Ontario, we have some bands of Indians who are very intelligent; we have members of these different bands who are just as intelligent as the average member of this House. I think it is almost a crime against everything that is fair to say to such a band of Indians: We will take possession of your reserve in defiance of treaty rights, without giving you an opportunity of being heard or even protesting as to whether you wish to surrender your reserve or not. The minister, a few nights ago, brought in a Bill before this House to confer upon him power to take a reserve in Victoria. That was a special case. I submit that in every such special case that may arise, where the Indians may refuse to surrender their reserve, yet, where it is in the pulblic interest that the Indian reserve should be surrendered, the Superintendent General can come down to parliament with a special Act. He need not take, as he proposes to do under this Bill, the broad power to apply this to every Indian reserve in Canada. It has always been our proud boast that we have treated our Indians fairly. But if this Bill becomes law we may sometimes have a Superintendent General who may not be as zealous for the best interest of the Indians as my hon. friend, yet in his hands would be placed the power to take any Indian reserve in Canada, within the scone of this Bill without giving the Indians the opportunity to make their protest felt. For these reasons, I think that the Bill should be referred to a committee for revision and elimination of some of these powers. If that is not done I would ask at least that the Indians may have the right to nominate the counsel who shall appear before this court to look after their interests.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not wish to traverse again the arguments on the general merits of the Bill. All these were thrashed out

840&
very fully when the Bill was up for consideration before, and the House in its wisdom decided that the principle should be adopted. With regard to the propriety of the Indians who object to the proposed readjustment of their affairs being authorized to name their counsel, I think that is a very dangerous proposal, and not in the interest of the Indians themselves. If the sound judgment of the Indians could be depended upon to be exercised in the protection of their own interests, then there would be no necessity for the Indian Act or for the supervision that parliament has placed over them. It is because it is recognized that they cannot be trusted to protect their own interests that this supervision is exercised, and I think it is within the judgment of the House that, under those circumstances to leave the question of the choice of a counsel to represent the Indians, in the hands of the judge of the Exchequer Court, is giving them better protection than to leave the matter at their own choice.
Does not subsection 1-a cover all the provisions of subsection 1 of the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not answer that off hand. -I substituted this section for the section of the old Act in the belief that this section met the present requirements better than the previous section.

The minister lias not done that. I do not see any provision repealing subsection 1 of the old Bill, and yet this seems to cover and go beyond the old section. This old section is inconsistent. It provides that no portion of any reserve shall be taken for the purpose of any railway, road or public work without the consent of the Governor in Council, and also that if any railroad, road or public work passes through or causes injury to any reserve, compensation must be paid; but it does not say in the latter case that they must have the consent of the Governor in Council, they may be trespassers. That is contradictory, but the section the minister has introduced now fully covers all the powers in the old section, and gives broader powers as well. Therefore, the old section is unnecessary and has not been repealed by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Bill has been referred back to committee, and I would ask it to remain in committee until I have had an opportunity of considering the point raised.

The phraseology of the present amendment is defective. You have the phrase : 'without the consent of the owner, may with such consent as aforesaid,' &c. That might be read that he shall Mr. OLIVER.
not take any land without the consent of the owner, and may with the consent of the owner. I 'think it is intended to refer to the-consent of the Lieutenant Governor in. Council, occurring earlier in the section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Undoubtedly that is the intention, and I think that would be the reading of the section.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to. and House went again into committee on the Bill.
On section 1,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think the objection of the hon. member for North Grey is well taken, but it may be overcome by a change of one word so that the introduction of section I would read:
Section 46 of the Indian Aot, chapter 81 of the Revised Statutes, 1908, is amended by substituting the following subsection for subsection 1 of the said section.
Then, in the following line, strike out the letter ' a ' after the figure '1

Would the minister include in his amendment that in subsection 1 the words: ' such consent ' where they occur in the seventh line be struck out, and .that in lieu thereof the words: ' consent of the Governor in Council ' be inserted?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That will be agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Could the minister inform the committee how many Indian reserves will be affected bv the wording of section 2?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not at the moment, but I think it is only the reserve situated in the city of Vancouver, although I may be mistaken.
How does the minister interpret the word 'adjoining'?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That the reserve line will touch the line of the corporation.

What is the object and purpose of drawing the line in that way? If the principle is good why not apply it to all reserves? I do not say that the principle should be applied but if you are taking such arbitrary power to remove reserves in this manner why not. apply it to all reserves? The same argument would apply to a rural district where an Indian reserve is situated, as would apply to a city, although perhaps not quite so strongly.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We recognize that the power asked for is arbitrary, and that it should not be exercised except under exceptional conditions, such exceptional conditions being that the land of the Indians,

by reason of their being contained within or adjoining a city, has reached an abnormal value altogether out of comparison with the original value or intention in the setting apart of the reserve, the result being that it is in the interest of the Indians that the townsite value which their reserve has attained should be translated into cash so that they may get the benefit of it rather than that they shall merely continue to occupy land having that value, but of which they are not getting the benefit.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
_ Mr. GRAHAM moved the second reading of Bill (No. 156) to amend the Department of Railways and Canals Act. He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of this Bill is to put upon the statute authority for the establishment of certain funds in connection with the management of the Intercolonial railway. As a matter of fact, these funds have been established in a way for some years. We have a fund, for instance, for the renewal of equipment, that is for the purchase of cars, and another for the renewal of rails. I want to establish one also to facilitate the payment of loss hy fire out of revenue where the loss should be paid out of the receipts of the road. In discussing this with the Finance Department, and with the Auditor General it was thought wise to amend the Act to give the department authority to establish these funds, so that there will be no question Irereafter about it or about the depositing of money in them, and the payment of money out of them.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Have you at present any trouble in providing renewal of equipment under your general vote? What is the necessity of a suspense account?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Each month we set apart a certain sum for this purpose, and if at the end of the financial year this money has not been expended it remains in the fund. The intention is to carry the account on, so that we will have it to pay for, say, work under contract.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: You are merely applying the money already voted to the intention of the appropriation?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Yes.	.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Does it mean that the minister has not to .come back for a revote, which has always been considered a salutary check? If the minister has $1,000,000 for a certain purpose, and he has spent $500,000 of it at the end of the year, he would now have to come back to parliament for a revote of the other $500,000? Does this propose that when once there is a vote of $1,000,000 there should be no reference to parliament again until he has expended that money, even though several years should elapse?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Hardly that. At present we lay aside $25,000 a month for railway equipment, and that is accounted for. Every railway company has to do something like that in order to carry on its business. The Auditor General thinks that possibly under the statute it is not clear he has the right to allow us to continue to do that. This money is merely to renew equipment out of railway revenue, and there would be little in the fund at the end of the year, but under the present system if there is $30,000 left, we have to pay it back to the consolidated fund and get it revoted.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The idea of the Bill Is probably all right. The minister gave me the impression that the money would not have to be revoted, but I do not see anything in the Bill which would enable him to use the money unless it were revoted. It is, I suppose, a proposal more in the way of keeping the accounts than touching the basis of parliamentary appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We have to keep to the rule in that respect.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: How does the Auditor General get rid of the audit of this money?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Every dollar expended has to be audited by the Auditor General, when we take a certain amount out of a vote to pay for cars, this makes it legal. He audits every account the same as now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: This Bill does not alter the law of appropriation?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I do not think so.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speechtext: Mr. GRAHAM moved the second reading of Bill (No. 150) to authorize the government of Canada to acquire by lease a certain line of railway in the province of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is the Bill we discussed very thoroughly on the resolution. The provincial government is guaranteeing the bonds of the St. John Valley railway to the extent of $25,000 a mile, and this Bill provides for its operation by the Intercolonial railway, provided it is constructed. I would like to have the Act on the statutes so that if an arrangement is made by the provincial government with any company we will be at liberty to enter into a contract with them.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, Bill read the 'second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

I would like to ask the Minister of Eailways and Canals if this clause is in accordance with the Act which was passed by the legislature of New Brunswick. I think that when the resolution was before us some objection was taken to the fact that equipment was not provided for in this Act while it was in the provincial Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I think there was a question as to the initial rolling stock, it being contended that -we had included the initial rolling stock in this Act, while it was not contemplated in the New Brunswick legislation. Personally I am not sure that it is absolutely necessary to retain the initial rolling stock. I find that it would be such a small matter in starting the new line that it is not worth while putting it in the way of the construction of the road or of its operation.
The minister would be willing to strike that out?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I would he willing to omit the rolling stock in order to help out the arrangement.

Will the minister state what is the difference in length between this new line and the Transcontinental line and its connection with St. John? Will he also state what the government have calculated tlhe loss would be, or the difference 'between what it would cost to run the road and the 60 per cent of the receipts which the government retain?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: My hon. friend the Minister of Railways has asked me to reply to the hon. gentleman, because I am familiar with the province of New Brunswick.
Have you ever heard of this railway before?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Yes, it has pleasant memories for me; I do not suppose I shall Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
ever forget it. This road runs from Grand Falls to St. John, by one of the routes surveyed by the engineers of the provincial government. The distance is 207 miles from Grand Falls to St. John. The Transcontinental goes from Grand Falls to Moncton, and from there the distance back to St. John is 88 miles.
What is the distance by the Transcontinental?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) says the distance from Grand Falls to Moncton is 198 miles. This, added to the 88 miles, would make the total distance from Grand Falls to St. John 286 miles. This line reduces the distance about 80 miles. I think the Minister of Railways can answer the question as to the loss better than I can.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I think it would be some years before the road would pay its way and pay the 60 per cent. I go further:	I
think that with the vast majority of branch lines in the maritime provinces that will always be found to be the case. I had not any idea, in making this proposition, that the Intercolonial railway would make a cent out of it. In fact, I have always thought that it would cost the Intercolonial a considerable sum of money to run this road on the 60 per cent ; but, looking at it from the point of view of the convenience of the people who for many years have not been able to get a line of railway through this valley, I thought the people of Canada would be prepared, even at a loss on the operation of the road, to agree to operate it on a 60 per cent basis.
Haven't they a line on the other side of the river running in the same direction between the two points?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: They have at certain points; but practically all the way from Woodstock to Fredericton it is 20 or 25 miles back from the river.
Is it much longer than this line?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
There is one road from Woodstock to St. John which first strikes McAdam. This must be 70 miles from the St. John river. From McAdam to St. John it also keeps away from the river until it reaches Welsford. For the last 14 miles it runs parallel with the river. There i3 another line from Fredericton to Woodstock running 20 or 25 miles from the river. But there is a very rich country from Woodstock to Fredericton, and also from Fredericton to Welsford, which is entirely without any accommodation. I would suggest that, with the unanimous consent

of the House, which I think would be necessary, the provision as to the company providing the initial equipment should be struck out. I am very glad indeed that the Minister of Railways feels that he can properly do that. It is exceedingly desirable that every reasonable effort should be made to secure the earliest construction of this line.
What does the Minister of Railways say? Will this interfere with the contract? '

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It will not. Take lino 17, and you will find the words ' with its appurtenances and rolling stock.' Strike out the word ' rolling stock.'

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is moved in amendment that the words ' rolling stock ' be struck out.

When the resolution upon which this Bill is founded was before the House I moved an amendment for the purpose of making the resolution agree with the Act passed by the New Brunswick legislature authorizing the Lieutenant Governor in Council to guarantee the bonds of the company. The objection I made to the resolution was that it did not follow the terms of section 1 of the New Brunswick Act. Section 1 of the New Brunswick Act provides that :
No swell agreement shall be entered into with any company or corporation for the construction of the 6aid line of railway or the guaranteeing of the said bonds, and no such bonds or debentures shall be guaranteed, unless and until the parliament of Canada shall enact legislation authorizing the granting of a subsidy in aid of the construction of the said railway to the amount of not less than $6,100 per mile, and authorizing the entering by the government of Canada into an independent agreement with such company or corporation and with the government of New Brunswick aforesaid, for the leasing of the 6aid line of railway, when completed, with its appurtenances and rolling stock and for the operation, equipment, maintenance, upkeep and repair by the said government of Canada, as part of the government railway system of Canada for a period of 99 years.
What I wished to have inserted was the word ' equipment.' I understand that the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Railways objected to the word ' equipment ' being inserted in the resolution, and it is not in the Bill. It seems to me that unless this Bill is made to correspond with the terms of the New Brunswick Act, the Lieutenant Governor in Council of New Brunswick will have no power to guarantee the bonds of the company. *

My hon. friend must bs in error. If he will read section 1, he will
find in it these words: ' Including the supply of additional rolling stock from time to time sufficient to handle the traffic as it may arise, maintenance, upkeep and repair.' It seems to me it is all provided in that section. In my opinion the resolution upon which this Bill is founded really followed the legislation of New Brunswick. I may be wrong, but if the Minister of Railways is willing to eliminate the question of initial rolling stock or rather take that away from the company which builds the road, I can see no reason why the Bill should not be agreed to, because the company must, out of its own funds or the funds received from the sale of bonds or the subsidy, provide for equipment as the Bill now stands. All thg Minister of Railways proposes is to eliminate the equipment so that it shall not be necessary for the company to make that expenditure, which makes it that much easier for the company to construct the road and have it operated by the Intercolonial railway.

My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) will see that these words in section 1 relating to rolling stock and operation are not in accord with the New Brunswick Act; and I do not see how the bonds can be guaranteed by the Governor in Council of New Brunswick until the condition prescribed by section 10 of the New Brunswick Act are fulfilled. That section requires an agreement for the operation, . equipment, maintenance, upkeep and repair by the government of Canada. The first section of this Bill differs from the New Brunswick Act in that it does not provide for the equipment of the railway by the government of Canada.

Even by the New Brunswick Act it is not required that the railway shall be equipped by the government of Canada, but that it shall be equipped by the company, and the company will then hand over to the government of Canada the road with its original equipment. This amendment proposes to relieve the company from the necessity of providing the initial equipment, and I cannot see that that would prevent the government of New Brunswick from guaranteeing the bonds.
