speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House in committee on Bill (No. 185) to amend the Fisheries Act.-Mr. Brodeur.
On section 1: licenses in British Columbia for making seal or fish oil,

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Mar-' ine and Fisheries).
speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
When the resolution on which this Bill is based was before the House I explained the object of the Bill. This clause is for the purpose of authorizing the minister to adopt some regulations governing the manufacture of oil from sea-lions, hair seals, sharks and dog-fish. As I explained the other day, we have had applications from people in British Columbia asking to be authorized to manufacture this product, provided regulations of this kind should be passed.
On section 2: license in British Columbia for salmon factories.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: This is a provision by which a license fee of $50 shall be charged to canneries in British Columbia. This has been recommended by the British Columbia Fish Commission as explained the other day when we were discussing the resolution.
Does this apply to the whole of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No, this part only applies to British Columbia.

I would like to ask the minister whether he has thought of the objection I made the other day, that this provision against dealing in salmon, and the curing thereof prevents a man curing salmon in his own back yard. Does the minister intend by this law to prohibit the individual fisherman from curing salmon? Is the law in the interest of large corporations who alone are able to pay this fee of $50?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It is not intended to prohibit any person from curing fish in his backyard for his own use. For the protection of the salmon canning industry generally, it is absolutely necessary that the fish should be canned and cured under hygienic conditions and one reason why a licence is provided for is that we may have some control over the method of canning and curing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: The minister says he does not want to prohibit a man curing his own fish, but as a matter of fact he does prohibit him under this clause, and I would suggest that he should so draft it that his intention be given effect to and that it should not prohibit a man from curing in his own house. I know where a man purposed curing salmon on his own premises, for his own use, and not for commercial purposes, and the officer of the department at New' Westminster told him that under this Act he required to take out a license which, the fee being $50, was prohibitive.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Was it for his own use?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: What the Act has in view are establishments that are curing or canning for commercial purposes.
The Act does not so limit it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: If the curing was for his own use I can see no objection to it, but certainly these large canneries ought to be licensed so we may see that they are conducted properly.

You can add the words,
' for commercial purposes.'
Mr. BRODEUF*. There \wbuld be no objection to that.

I agree that the government should have such control over large canning establishments as will enable them to ensure that the canning is carried on under sanitary conditions. But, when you add the word ' curing ' it means pickling salmon or smoking salmon, and w'hen a person buys pickled or smoked fish he can see what he is buying and there is not the same necessity for taking precautions as in the case of canning. I do not see why a man should have to pay a license fee of $50 because he is going to smoke salmon or put it in barrels even for commercial purposes. Of course the Act does not apply to the Atlantic coast and the people of British Columbia know what they want.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The curing establishments we have in mind in British Columbia are large establishments which do not exist in the maritime provinces and they can easily stand a fee of $50. In some cases the curing and canning is carried on in the same establishment. In order to meet the objection raised by the hon. member for New Westminster, I am willing that we should add the words, ' for commercial purposes.'

I have diffidence in venturing on this subject, not being a salmon fisherman, but I would ask the minister if these canning establishments are carried on by persons who themselves catch the fish? The minister limits the operation of this Act to the province of British Columbia, and I more than doubt that this parliament has power to regulate trade and commerce in a particular province, because that does not seem to come within the general regulation of trade and commerce confided to us under the British North America Act. If this legislation is under the provision which gives the parliament of Canada control of the inland and coast fisheries, then I do not see how a man who buys salmon and proceeds to can has anything to do with the fishing. It looks to me as if this provision were in the nature of local legislation for British Columbia, as to how people will carry on a particular kind of business in that province.
You might as well provide for a license to can chickens.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Under section 91 of the British North America Act we have the right to regulate the fisheries, and we consider that the number of canning establishments has an effect on the preservation of the fish, because the larger the number of such establishments the greater the number of fish caught. In regulating the canneries we regulate to a certain extent the quantity of fish taken. In most cases in British Columbia the canners also cure the fish. It was the unanimous recommendation of the commission that legislation of this kind should be passed in order to preserve the fisheries.

I quite understand that parliament has power to make regulations to preserve the fisheries, but this seems to me to be a somewhat remote method of getting at it. Instead of restricting in some way the quantity of fish to be caught, we take it upon ourselves to prescribe regulations requiring a man to take out a license for a canning establishment, and we actually prescribe that there shall be not more than one such establishment within 50 miles. You are regulating the quantity of fish to be taken by the indirect method of imposing obligations on people who are carrying on businesses in which they handle fish, but w'hich do not seem to me to form any part of the fisheries. If you carried that principle out to its logical conclusion, you might prescribe how many fish stalls there should be on the market in Montreal. It would all work back -to the preservation of the fisheries. It seems to be doubtful whether this is an Act to regulate the fisheries, as you are 266 h
regulating how the fish shall be handled after they have passed out of the fishermens' hands.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The salmon of British Columbia is not like the salmon on the Atlantic coast, a large quantity of which is sold in a fresh condition. The sock-eye salmon has to be canned to be placed on the market. Therefore, to reduce the quantity of fish to be caught, which we consider necessary for the preservation of the fisheries, we think the best method is to regulate the number of canning establishments, so that they will not be more numerous than the fisheries can stand. I may say also that we recently came to an agreement with the British Columbia government by which a certain number of fishing boats could be.licensed in that province. As a result of our researches, we think this is the best way to conserve the fisheries.
As regards the number of boats to do the fishing, that would seem to me to be a p'art of the fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Canning is just as important.

No doubt it is just as important; but when the Act gave you the control of the sea-coast and inland fisheries, did it also give you the right to control the fish after they were caught, and to determine how many should be canned in a particular province? If it did, it seems to me that it would give you the right to determine how many fish any man should eat, because that would work back to the protection of the fisheries.
Suppose the province, for revenue purposes, imposed a tax of $50 or $100 on each of these establishments, where would you be then?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I may inform my hon. friend that Jhey. are imposing a tax to-day.
The provincial government might also impose a license.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes, there is no doubt that under the British North America Act the provincial government could impose a license, and it is doing so.

I would like to point out to the minister again, as I did the other day, that the effect of this clause is not in any way to preserve the fisheries of British Columbia, that it makes no difference to the fishermen who go out with their nets to catch fish, how many salmon canneries are licensed, that the only effect of this provision is to strengthen the monopoly in the production of this article of food. The regulation providing that no canning establishment may be conducted without a license, coupled

with the policy that no license shall be granted to any person not already in the business, continues in British Columbia the monopoly in the salmon-canning business now established; it does not operate to the preservation of the fish, but does operate to the increase of the profits of the canners at the expense of the fishing population of British Columbia. It creates a condition peculiar to that province, and not prevailing in the state of Washington where there are canners independent of the fishing combine. Now, I appeal to the minister to take further information on this subject if he is not possessed of it. I told him the other day, what seemed to be news to him, that there is in British Columbia an absolute fish combine; that all interests there are joined to establish the price which they will pay the fishermen, and the price at which they will sell, and to make for themselves whatever profits they see fit. I told him that this operates harshly on the fishing population, because they had in many instances to destroy_ a great portion of their catch, and I appeal to him before he puts this Bill through, to make provision in cases of that kind that when the licensed canners would not buy the fish which the fishermen caught, they should have some other market in which to sell them. I reminded him also that he not only prevented them selling their fish on the Canadian side by limiting the number of licenses, but also prescribed an absolute prohibition of export ; so that when a Canadian fisherman has 400 or 500 fish in his boat ready to sell, and no Canadian canner will buy them, and when an American canner a few miles away holds out his hand for those fish, 'the minister says, I prohibit you by force of law taking those fish across the boundary line. That is the condition at present. It does not preserve the fish.	On the
contrary, it makes the cruel enactment that a man with this valuable property in his possession must destroy it because this government will not allow him to sell it in any quarter. It does not preserve the fish, but attacks the livelihood of the fishermen. In this respect the Canadian government is fostering as tight a monopoly in the production of food as any monopoly in the world. In the enactment of this law we confirm in cold blood what was perhaps an accident at the outset. We are providing absolutely that men with valuable property must destroy that property without getting any benefit to themselves, and for the profit of the salmon canners. The minister gives as a reason for this prohibition (hat the salmon canning establishments are also curing establishments; but if that is his only reason his purpose will be served by licensing them as canning establishments simply.	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
There are some which are only curing establishments.
' Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster). There are private individuals who wish to go into the curing busines on their domestic premises, but who are prohibited by this because they cannot pay the license_ fee in competition with the large associations. We find the Minister of Fisheries standing up for the capitalists against the fishermen. The minister should be of all men the first to stand by the poor fisherman who is not able to protect himself. As I see no good that can result from the prohibition of curing salmon without a special license, but much evil, and as, so far as the canners are concerned, every good purpose is served by licensing their establishments as canneries, I move that the words ' or salmon curing establishments * be struck out of the section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: My hon. friend's statement with regard to the combine is not at all well founded.
In what respect is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Because there are several establishments. Take the Fraser river for example, Some are under the control of the British Columbia Packers Association, but there are also several independent concerns who are competing with the larger establishments, and doing fairly well.
Will the hon. minister give the names of any of these concerns?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes, we must have in the department the names of those independent concerns. My hon. friend himself said the other day that there were some.
I would like to know the names of any which the minister has in his mind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I am giving the hon. gentleman himself as an authority because the other day he said that there were besides the British Columbia Packers Association some independent concerns. He claimed, however, that most of those independent concerns, and the British Columbia Packers' Association had a sort of board of trade or association like the Manufacturers Association,' dealing with their interests generally. I do not suppose that any one would say that the manufacturers are a monopoly because they are members of an association called the Canadian Manufacturers Association. I understand that, so far as the Fraser river canneries are concerned, there is a large company, and some other independent companies which have absolutely independent management,

and I do not see why we should call them a monopoly. I may say also that we are not prevented by this legislation from issuing a license to any other company, or association which shows its ability to carry on a curing or canning establishment. Quite the reverse. My hon. friend said the other day that it was pretty evident there was a combine regulating the prices to be paid to the fishermen. Of course if there were any such close combine among the canners, the department would be anxious to come to the rescue of the fishermen, and give them or give any other association a license. We are taking the power to grant licenses simply in order to control more effectively those cannery establishments. To-day we have no control over them. I would be very glad to refuse a license to any company which would go into a combine to the injury of the fishermen. So that instead of opposing this legislation, my hon. friend, who has the interests of the fishermen at heart, should help the government to have it put on the statutes. If there be no legislation at all, what can be done to prevent those men combining amongst themselves? There are, of course, some general laws, but they could not be applied so effectively as this legislation. I might remind my hon. friend that some years ago we passed a law obliging manufacturers to take out a license, and providing that if they should combine to prevent the freedom of trade, we could refuse them licenses. In like manner if those canners should combine for the purpose of depriving the fishermen of their honest, fair profit, it would be the duty of the government to refuse them licenses; and when those people see that they might be deprived of their licenses, they will be careful about forming any such combine.

What advice would the minister give now to a fisherman-and this is not a hypothetical case-who catches five or six hundred fish and brings them down to the cannery wharf, and finds a notice put up by the licensed canners to the effect that the limit to-day is 200 fish? What is the fisherman to do with the other three or four hundred?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: In such a case, these men should immediately apply for a license and they will get it.

No doubt, the minister means that. But I would point out to him that it takes perhaps six or seven months at the shortest to get the machinery for a salmon cannery, and the life of the salmon after it is caught is about one day. Therefore, it is simply impossible for the man who brings his six hundred fish to the salmon cannery and finds all but 200 of them left on his hands
to secure relief by applying for a license to start a cannery. I wish to tell the minister that the effect of this limitation is not to preserve the fish but to make it necessary that a large quantity of fish must be absolutely destroyed. His combine of canners refuse to buy the fish, the minister will not license any other canners, nor will he permit the export of the fish to the canners on the American side who are perfectly willing to buy these fish at any time. The fishermen can get absolutely no relief from the minister. He protects the combine at every point but refuses to protect the fisherman. I do not think the minister understands the situation. I think if he were on the ground and saw, as I have seen over and over again, large quantities- of as fine fish as ever were caught dumped into the river, he would hesitate little about making the necessary regulations. I can assure the minister the effect of these regulations is absolutely cruel to the fishermen of the Fraser, and that 'they do not operate to preserve the fish but rather to destroy them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) ought to be fair and state to the House why it is that, occasionally, there is a larger catch of fish than can be handled in one day. He has stated that he has seen fishermen come in with four or five hundred fish of which the cannery man would take only one hundred and the other three or four hundred would have to be dumped into the river. I believe it is a fact that on several occasions during the big runs such conditions have existed, because the catch for the day, or for several days in succession, was so great that the canneries could not possibly handle the fish during the twenty-four hours or so which elapse before they spoil. Therefore it was that the surplus had to be dumped into the river. That has occurred on the Fraser during abnor mal runs in a big year. It is understood that the big run comes once in four years But in the last fourth year the run was not so large as to bring about these conditions, while in the ordinary years there are not enough fish to keep the canneries operating. Consequently no new canneries have started. The hon. member (Mr. Taylor) says the policy of the department is to keep down the number of canneries, and so it brings about a condition of monopoly. As a matter of fact there have been no applications for canneries on the Fraser river for a number of years. I am quite sure that if my hon. friend or any of his friends want a license for a cannery on the river, the minister will give the subject his best consideration. The hon. gentleman knows that many canneries are not operated, including some owned by

the British Columbia Packers. They have been closed down. That has been true for a number of years. But it was unfair to convey the impression to the House that a large number of fish are being dumped into the river as a consequence of the policy of the department in limiting the number of canneries. Every person who has visited the canneries knows that ordinarily, in every fourth year the run is so great that the canneries cannot pack all the fish, and, therefore, take a certain number from each fisherman, which is fair. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor, New Westminster) said something about the prohibition of the export of salmon taken by British Columbia fishermen

that the fishermen are not permitted to sell them to the cannery men on the American side, which would mean the cannery men on the Sound. But that would operate two ways. If the Fraser river fish caught by Canadian fishermen can be taken over and sold to the American cannery men-they would only have a distance of twenty miles or so to go-then the salmon caught in enormous quantities in the traps on the American side of the line should be permitted to come into British Columbia canneries to be canned there. The hon. gentleman knows that th4 prohibition of the export of fish for that purpose on the Fraser, and the prohibition of the importation of fish to the canneries of that river was agreed to a number of years ago. I believe it is more in the interest of the Fraser fishermen than it is of the Fraser river cannery men. The cannery men especially would be anxious to have it removed, so that they could go down to the traps across the line and buy all the fish they want. The hon. gentleman says these fish are thrown away. That is not always the case. I know, that as a matter of fact, large quantities of fish-I think a whole steamer load-was taken from the Fraser river to a northern cannery to be canned. The hon. gentleman says there is a monopoly among the cannery men of British Columbia. I do not believe there is.
On the Fraser river, there is a combination of cannery men during the season which regulates, as far as the cannervmen can regulate, the price to be paid for fish. That may be a combination, no doubt it is to that extent. But the Fraser river is not the only fishing district in British Columbia; there are more canneries outside of the Fraser than on the Fraser, and there are very many independent cannery men who are not in the British Columbia Packers, which is a group of canners working as one company. There is the Bell-Irving Co., a large, 'strong company, outside the British Columbia Packers' Co. In the Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
north you have the Wallace Bros., absolutely independent of the British Columbia Packers. Then there is Henry Doyle, J. H. Todd & Son, the original cannery men of the province. These men are not in the British Columbia Packers; they are scattered over the coast from Alaska to the boundary line of the United States, and it is idle to say there is a combination that is operating to the disadvantage of the fishermen or to the enhancement of the price of such a food product as fish. Of course most of our fish is sold in Europe, the consumption in Canada is very small, and the surplus of the United States goes to the English market, where we have to meet it in competition. There is no doubt that the cannery men on the Fraser get together and agree what price they will pay the fishermen for their fish. The price may start at 10 cents, and if it is a scarce year prices go up to 25 cents per salmon, according to the abundance or scarcity of the fish. The cannery men agree that they will pay a uniform price. To that extent there is a combination and that operates against the fishermen. On the other hand, the fishermen combine and say; We will not sell ibelow a certain price. As a matter of fact, the fishermen and the cannery men agree that a fair price shall be paid; in scarce years a high price and in plentiful years a low price. I would suggest that in order not to interfere with the fisherman who wants to cure fish, the words ' for commercial purposes ' should be inserted after ' British Columbia,' so that small curing establishments would not be included as curing establishments and be required to pay the license fee of $50.

I have no fault to find with the conclusion at which the minister has arrived, but I must take exception to many of the statements he made on his way to (hat conclusion. I have no objection to curing establishments for commercial purposes being licensed and taxed in this way, but I have very serious objection to what has occurred in the past, that is individual fishermen desiring to cure on a modest scale being refused permission to do so unless they took out a license and paid the same fee as a cannery with a large pack. The minister is far from being posted on the condition of the salmon industry in British Columbia, evidently he has given very little attention to it. I would suggest to him that it is not fair to those who are posted upon the salmon canning industry that he, with his prestige as a minister, should in this House contradict the testimony founded on facts which we are in a position to give. No one stated in this House, what he is at such pains to controvert, that the

British Columbia Packers' Association control the industry in British Columbia or on the Fraser river. Five or six times the minister has made the statement that the British Columbia Packers are not the only persons in the industry in British Columbia. I have never heard any one say they were, in fact in the discussion the othex day in the minister's absence that fact "was made quite plain to every person here. There are on the Fraser river, for instance, three important interests, the British Columbia Packers Association, the A. B. C. Canners Association, the St. Mungo Cannery, and one or two others, all . entirely distinct as to ownership and management, but all merged into one absolute combine as to the price to be paid for fish, and as to the price at which they will sell their product. The minister, when enlightening the committee just now, knew about the existence of these three separate associations of canners; evidently he did not know that these three were combined to fix buying and selling prices. In the absence of that knowledge, it is unfair to come to the House and say that no combine exists. Such a combine does exist, not sub rosa, not secretly, but openly; the combination has a public office and a public secretary; it issues to the press as well as to the members of the association day by day and week by week, during the canning season, its reports. We all know of its existence and it amazes me that the minister should say that no such combination exists. I must assume he does it innocently, I believe he does it unintentionally, but it is dangerous for him out of the mass of his misinformation or lack of information to contradict statements made to this committee by way of information. It is idle for the minister to say there is no destruction of fish. We on the scene, on the Fraser river, knows that this goes on all the time, and that the fishermen are absolutely helpless in the face of it. There is no notice given in advance of any limitation to be placed by the canners on the purchase of fish. The fishermen are sent out by the canners to catch all the fish they can get. They go to work at dark, they remain fishing until dawn; they may be rewarded with several hundred fish, and the first intimation they have that they are not to be paid for all their catch is when they arrive at the cannery wharf and see a notice that only a limited quantity of fish, it may be 100 or 200, or any other number arbitrarily fixed, will be bought by that cannery. I say to the minister and his colleague from British Columbia that any fisherman arriving at a wharf who is confronted by that notice has absolutely no recourse.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Does that limitation of the number of fish apply to every year, or is ii only occasional?

The limitation as to the number of fish is put up by the cannery owners at any moment when it suits their purpose to put it up, and that is where the hardship comes in, that there is no certainty on the part of any fisherman when he catches fish that he will have any market for them. The minister does not seem to know that American fish from traps are imported.
At six o'clock, Committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On section 2,

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose, I was pointing out a few inaccuracies in the statement, then just made, by the minister from British Columbia. Amongst other matters the minister referred to the fact that under certain conditions fish caught in the traps on the American side might be imported into British Columbia. The minister referred to this possible importation of trap-caught fish as something to be discouraged at all hazards. It so happens that such fish have all along been imported, are every season imported and are canned in the canneries on the Fraser river. This is a sample of how extensive was the knowledge brought to bear on this subject by the minister who undertook to tell the committee that I was astray on the information that I handed out. Under*the law as it has stood the fishermen are absolutely prohibited from selling their fish on the American side. They are prohibited from exporting it a! all, but the canners have not been prohibited from importing fish. Upon bringing it into the country, it is true, they pay a duty, but as they export the greater part of their product, that duty, minus a very small charge for office fees, is always refunded to them, so that the transaction costs them nothing more than putting up a cheque from the time they bring the fish into the country until the time they export it. The minister from British Columbia, when he mentioned this as something wdiieh at all hazards should be prohibited, overlooked the fact that he is giving his warm, enthusiastic, cordial approval to the arrangement which has been malde at Washington whereby that which he says should not be brought into the country at all, is to be admitted, not of our own volition, but is to be admitted

without any right on our part to interfere in any way with the process under the terms of this treaty, and is to be admitted free of duty. I would ask the minister what he thinks of that and upon what ground he can justify the attitude which he took here to-day of admiration for what he thought was the prohibition of the importation of that fish for canning with his attitude as a member of the government in bringing into effect 'a 'solemn bargain made with the authorities at Washington, whereby we are compelled to admit fish and have no means of keeping it out of our country unless we abro gate that arrangement.
There is another matter as to which I would like to say a word. It was the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I think, who referred to this. In answer to my objection that under the regulations as they stand, fishermen are often compelled to destroy their fish, because the canners on the Fraser river have not the capacity to can them and put a limit on the catch, the minister reminded me that these fish are often taken on scows to the Skeena river, there to be canned, and he instanced this as a proof that there is no limitation upon the catch such as I have suggested. The minister omitted to state what is the fact, that when the fish are so bought for transportation to the Skeena river, they are bought at a greatly reduced price, so that the canner gets just as much profit from canning on the Skeena as he would if he canned on the Fraser, but the unfortunate fisherman gets a half or less price compared with that which he would get if there were facilities for canning on the Fraser river. I would like to direct his attention also to a circumstance connected with the restriction permitting only a limited number of licences to be issued to the canners, because he will see that the effect of that supposed precaution on his part for the preservation of the fishery is altogether destroyed so long as persons having a license to can on the Fraser are permitted to take a whole scow load of fish away from that district and can them at far distant places when their licenses were only supposed to apply to fish canned on the Fraser. I would like to point out to the minister also, to show how delusive is the idea that the catch of fish is limited by the number of licenses issued, that canneries vary a great deal in capacity, that under this Act, as I understand it- he may correct me if I am wrong-a cannery of the largest, capacity pays the same license as a cannery of the most limited capacity, and that the process of enlarging canneries is so simple that an establishment that has but one unit this year may, next season, consist of two, three, or Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster).
four units under the same control. Under the regulations now in force, if we have twelve canneries this year of one unit capacity each, we may have next year, under the same license, twelve canneries of four units each, or forty-eight units, making four times the quantity of fish that they may can, and yet the minister states that he is preventing the fish from being caught by prescribing that only the twelve present holders of licenses shall have licenses next year. I ask him what difference it makes to the fish whether we have twelve canneries of four units each or forty eight canneries of ;one unit each. jThe capacity would be precisely the same, but the monopoly created by the minister under the present regulations would be entirely destroyed. I think the time is opportune now, when the Bill is before us, for the minister to give this his serious consideration, so that when the fishermen complain, this year or next year, of being unable to sell their fish, they will not be told that an unconsidered provision of the law has brought about this condition, because here we have the whole subject up for review, the minister is fully informed of the present working of his Act, he has abundant opportunity now to correct the evil, he has noticed it and not more than three or four minutes would be required to remove all these disabilities to which I have referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor, New Westminster), has only one object and that is to establish the fact-if it were a fact-that in some manner or other the department has, by its enactments and regulations, created a monopoly in the fishing industry in British Columbia. I desire to say that is not correct at all. The hon. gentleman stated that all the proprietors of the canneries in British Columbia were in what is known as the British Columbia Canners Association.
I have heard that of the British Columbia Canners' Association, and I certainly could not have said so.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The Fraser River Canners' Association was merged in whit is known as the British , Columbia Canners' Association which includes probably one-half of the canners in the province of British Columbia. On the. Fraser river where twelve canneries operated last year, eight of these canneries were in the British Columbia Canners' Association, and four were not. The names of the independent canners are:	Todd and Sons, Lee Company, Great West Packing Company, and Glen Rose Packing Company. There were twelve canneries operating on the Fraser

river, but about three times that number must have closed up because there was not fish enough to go round and probably most of these canneries are owned by the firms who are now operating canneries, particularly the British Columbia Packers. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor, New Westminster) has tried to establish the fact that the canners of British Columbia were combined in an association to regulate the price they shall buy the fish for, and the price they shall sell the fish at. That is not correct, inasmuch as of the 39 canneries that operated in British Columbia last year, only 20 were members of the British Columbia Canners' Association, and 19 were independent or outside the association. The report I have here comes from the secretary of the British Columbia Canners' Association, and is authoritative, and it shows that on the Skeena river-my hon. friend confines his attention to the Fraser river, but that is not the whole of the fishing industry in British Columbia by any means -on the Skeena river there are four members of the association, and four who are not, the independent canners toeing Todd and Sons, Kildala Packing Company, Wallace Brothers, Limited, and the Skeena River Commercial Company. At Rivers Inlet, there are three members of the association, and three who are not, the latter being Todd and Sons, Kildala Packing Company, Strathcona Packing Company. At Naas river two are members of the association, and two are not; in the outlying districts there are three members of the Canners' Association, and six outside or independent. The fact is, therefore, that one-half of the canners operating in British Columbia are not members of this so-called combine. But as a matter of fact the British Columbia Canners' Association is not a combine in the ordinary sense. As I understand it they are organized largely for the purpose of giving attention to the fishery regulations, keeping in touch with the Department of Fisheries with regard to the fishing regulations, and generally for looking after their own interests. It is true, as my hon. friend says, that at the opening of the fishing season the cannery men regulate if they can the price they are going to pay for the fish during the year, but on the other hand the fishermen who have a union, get together and try to keep the price at a higher rate, and by mutual concession the price is fixed. If the fish are plentiful the price is low, probably ten cents per fish, and if the fish are very scarce the price is high. I have known it to be 25 cents per fish, but I am not very well informed as to the prices. There is no evidence further than I have explained, of a combine to regulate the price paid. The remarks of my hon. friend appply to the Fraser river a little more than
to the other districts. On the northern rivers it is true that more Japanese and Indians are engaged, in the fishing industry than on the Fraser river where more white men are employed. With respect to the importation of fish for canning purposes, I am aware that some years ago it was a common thing for canners south of the boundary to come into Canadian waters and buy the fish caught on the Canadian side. That was objected to because some of the fishermen were under agreement to sell the fish to our own canners, and it was also undesirable that fish caught in Canadian -waters should be taken south of the line to bd canned in American canneries and form a portion of their pack. On the other hand some of our cannery men have gone south of the boundary line when fish were scarce in Canadian waters, and bought large qtfantities from the American traps and canned them at their canneries. That was a mutual interchange of fish. Some years ago the department prohibited the importation of fish from the American traps to be canned in our canneries; the Canadian fishermen having objected to the competition. On the other hand, our fishermen claimed the right to sell their fish to the Americans, if they could get a better price than they were getting from the Canadian canners. After a while the practice was stopped and there was no more selling of Canadian fish caught toy Canadian fishermen to be canned in the American canneries. It is quite true that Canadian cannery men can go south of the boundary and buy all the fish they like and pay one cent a pound duty, and bring them to the canneries, and they can export them and probably get a rebate of the duty paid, although my information is that there is nothing of that kind done at the present time. As a matter of fact considering the catch of fish south of the boundary line there is none to sell to the Canadian canneries. If my information is correct that sort of importation of fish for canning purposes has not occurred for years. Tn my view our fish ought to be canned in our own country, and my friend -will admit that if we permit our canners to go to the American traps and buy fish to can in Canadian canneries it would be competing with the catch of the Canadian fishermen and lowering the price of their fish. But, if our cannery men can buy fish from the American traps and bring them into Canada, and pay one cent a pound duty and export that fish and get a rebate of the amount of the duty. I would say to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that our fishermen ought to be treated equally favourably and be given the advantage of selling their fish to American canners. I do not think the practice prevails at all,

and I think my hon. friend -will have some difficulty in establishing that fact.

1 think I made it abundantly plain that 1 was speaking for the fishermen of my riding, who are the fishermen on the Fraser river, and the Minister of Fisheries seems to be engaged in the rather dubious occupation of drawing a herring across this salmon trail. I made no reference to the fisheries on the Skeena river, which are entirely different from those on the Fraser. The .seasons are different, the prices are different, the classes of people employed are different, the methods of the canneries are different. The two fisheries are entirely distinct. The canners on the Fraser river are combined under the name of the Fraser River Canners' Association, or \vhatever modification of that, name has been recently made, as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries told me the other day was the case. The combine is as tight now as it ever was, and was equally so last season. The usual notice was issued at the beginning of the season by all ttie canners that the canners of the Fraser river would pay such prices for fish, and the same prices prevailed in all the canneries on the Fraser river last season. There is a fish cannery combine, and if the minister does not know about it, I would advise him to pay due attention to the situation there, and the fact will be very soon forced upon his attention. It is nothing to the fishermen on the Fraser river that some of the operators of traps on the coast of Vancouver Island are not in the combine; neither is it anvthing to them that the conditions are different on the Skeena river. We are concerned about the combine on the Fraser river, and what we ask of the minister is. not that he shall issue more licenses on the Skeena river or allow more traps on the coast of Vancouver Island, but ti.at if any of our interests on the Fraser river desire to open a new cannery, they may be permitted to get a license.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend if he knows of any person on the Fraser river or anywhere else who desires to establish another cannery on the Fraser river?

Yes, I have known of it, and when they have gone to the Fisheries office at New Westminster and made the preliminary inquiries-because you cannot establish a cannery in a day just as you buy a hat-they have been told that the decision of the department was that no new licenses should be issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I want to say, then, to my hon. friend that if any decent company wants to establish another cannery on the Fraser river, and makes application to the department for a license, it will have my strong commendation, and I have the word of my hon. friend the minister that he will give it fair consideration.
Am I to understand that the explanation of all these large words is that there is to be free trade in canning licenses?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: What my hon. friend is afraid of, I understand, is monopoly. He is afraid that this legislation is going to bring monopoly. I may tell him that it is quite the reverse. There may be to-day monopoly to a certain extent, though there is not practically, because, as has been stated by my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue, there are on the Fraser river a certain number of canners who are outside and independent of the Association. These companies have formed an association for the purpose of approaching the government and discussing the various questions affecting the fisheries generally, just as we have in all parts of the country various persons engaged in the same trade who have formed an association for the purpose of discussing their mutual interests. That does not mean that they have formed a monopoly. Nobody would say that all the members of the Manufacturers' Association should be called monopolists. I may say to my hon. friend that if there are some people who want a license, and who cannot get justice from the existing canners, they will be welcome; and if on any occasion it is proven that justice has not been rendered to the fishermen, and those fishermen want to form an association and establish a cannery, they will be welcome to a license. The legislation we are proposing to-day is to kill any monopoly. If the canners do not render justice to the fishermen, why should we be called upon to renew their licenses? To-day the ordinary rules of trade are regulating these canneries; there may be a large number or a small number; but in future every cannery will have to come to the government for a license; and if it is found that they do not treat the fishermen fairly and equitably, we shall have an opportunity to force them to render justice. My hon. friend, who claims to be a friend of the fishermen, should welcome this legislation as being in the right direction.

The hon. minister says that if cofnplaint were made against the present canners, he would not renew their licenses. Suppose the fishermen made complaint against all the pre-

sent canners, and the minister refused to rene'w their licensee, how much fetter off would the fishermen be? They would be much worse off. What the fishermen want is not that the minister should interfere with the canners, but that he should cease interfering with other people. Then they will toe able to keep the canners straight without the minister's intervention. If the canners ill-use the fishermen this year, and the fishermen organize next year to meet the conditions, the canners, with their powerful combination and unlimited capital will so alter the conditions next year as to freeze out the new people, and when they are frozen out, the canners will revert to the old conditions. That is the experience with all combinations of that kind. I would like to point out how weak is the minister's comparison with the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, because there is no license or any other condition required before an investor can have a factory, and create the conditions which entitle him to become a member of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. There is absolute free trade in factories. All the manufacturers do not belong to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and if any outside investor sees a chance of engaging in a business now controlled by any person in that association, he is at perfect liberty to do so.
Whereas in the ease of the fisheries, no person ambitious to go into that business can do so unless he has a license from the minister; and for years it has been the policy of the minister to refuse a license to any one outside of those already engaged in the industry. He refers to the fact that many canneries on the Fraser are idle. But *why are they idle? Because to create a monopoly, all the canneries on that river which could be purchased, were purchased by the British Columbia Packers' Association. Speaking from memory they purchased about fifty canneries and immediately closed about thirty of them. In New Westminster we had several cannery sites held under long leases from the city, but unfortunately the city did not foresee the possibility of outside capital coming in and buying out those concerns for the purpose of closing them. The British Columbia Packers' Association did close those canneries and made a condition in re-leasing the property that no canneries should be established on it. That was a profitable move from the standpoint of the association, but it did great injustice to the fishermen on the Fraser and the city of New Westminster. The hon. minister loses sight of the fact that all those interests are combined when there is question of fixing the price which will be paid the fishermen for their fish. He knows that in the last big
year, when our fishermen might have expected to make a profitable harvest, the price of salmon on the Canadian side was exactly one half of the price which the same people were paying on the American side for identical salmon at the same time. When we got 10 cents per fish, the American fishermen got 20 cents; and when we got 124 cents' per fish, the American fishermen got 25 cents. My hon. friend's department alone is responsible for this condition, and it is a condition which we have only this opportunity of amending before the next big run is on.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I am extremely sorry to find that my hon. friend still reiterates the statement that there is a combine in British Columbia, and that the fishermen are not well treated. If there be a combine, how does he account for the fact that there are several men in the business who are not in the association, but are absolutely independent of it? Besides, how is it that during the last three years no one applied for a license for the opening of any new cannery? Several establishments have been closed and my hon. friend says they were closed for the purpose of monopoly. That is contrary to the information we have in the department. The information we have is that these establishments were closed because they did not pay. But if other people wanted to start canneries, why did they not apply for a license? Within the last three years, not one has applied for a license.
My information is to the contrary.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: That is the information I have from the officers of the department.

The local inspector does not necessarily report applications for licenses. He has to inform prospective applicants that there is no use in his doing so because he has orders from the minister that no licenses are to be given.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: If the inspector had an application he would send it to the department. The inspector out there is a very efficient man, who would not refuse a license without referring the application to the department.
Is it not a fact that the minister notified the inspector that no new licenses were to be issued?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No, we never gave any notification to that effect.

I certainly was under that impression. That was stated in this House last year in the course

of the session and was not contradicted by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: That is not the information I have from the Acting Superintendent of Fisheries. He says that he never gave such instructions.
If the minister will say that we shall have free trade in fishing licenses in the future, and that he will give a license to any one who wants to establish a cannery, that will be satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I shall be very glad to consider any application for a license. So far we have never had any.
The minister has never refused an application?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No.
Why, then, will my hon. friend not remove this harmful impression by saying that he will not refuse a license in any case without some good reason?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Certainly any man who applies for a license and proves that it is necessary such a license should be given, will get it.

But how can any one prove it is necessary? How can any one tell what the future catch will be? We do not know what fish may be caught. It is an absolutely impossible premise which the minister lays down, and that justifies my suggestion that the reason he will not promise free trade in licenses is because he does not intend to grant new licenses.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that if he has any one who wants a license, let him make the application and it will be duly considered; and if he makes out a good case the license will be granted.

I am not here as the advocate of any special privilege or as an applicant for a special privilege for any one. I am speaking for the whole public and maintaining the rights of the fishermen to free trade in salmon licenses.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment is that the words ' Or salmon curing ' be struck out of subsection 23a of section 2.
Amendment negatived.
The hon. minister from British Columbia (Mr. Templeman) suggested an amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I move to add after the words ' British Columbia ' the words ' for Mr. TAYLOR.
commercial purposes ' to subsection 23a of section 2.
Does the minister intend to extend this system to the curing of other varieties of fish, and to other , parts of Canada than British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: That is not the intention now.

That is not the intention under this Bill, but let us understand whether, this principle having been adopted by this parliament, the minister will, later on, introduce legislation w'hich. would enable him to place under license any fish curing establishment in any part of Canada, no matter what variety of fish it might handle or what conditions had prevailed up to that time in regard to them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
It is not the intention of the department now to make any change of that kind.
Section 2, as amended, agreed to.
On section 3-amending section 36-annual fee for lobster cannery license.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: This clause is inserted as a result of the recommendation last year of the Committee on Marine and Fisheries.

What protests have been received by the department in respect to any of the recommendations made by the Committee on Marine and Fisheries last year concerning the lobster fishery? I understand from statements in the press that protests ""have been made against certain of the recommendations, and, indeed, against some of the regulations framed under the recommendations, more especially that relating to the standard trap. It seems to me, inasmuch as that committee made this report, all the suggestions they did make were to be accepted in their entirety, and any suggestion which they made had reference one to the other. So, if it is not the intention of the department to enforce the matter of standard traps, it seems to me questionable whether it would be the intention of the committee that these other provisions, especially the increase in regard to the license fee should be enforced.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
So far as the change proposed in this section is concerned I believe mo protest has come from any person or company. Some protests were made concerning the date at which we should put in force the regulations concerning the traps. My hon. friend will remember that these questions came up at the opening of this session. (I was going to

say last session, because we have already 6pent some days upon this matter.) I thought I could not deal with these protests without having the matter referred to the Committee on Marine and Fisheries, as all the regulations that had been adopted were adopted upon the recommendation of the committee. Consequently, this complaint was referred to the committee. But the committee recommended -I think unanimously, but at any rate by a large majority-that the change asked for in the date of the coming into force of the regulations should be adopted.. This Teport was made to the House, and as a Tesult of that report I had the regulations amended to cover the recommendations of the committee. Since then I do not remember any complaint made to the department with regard to these recommendations. Perhaps I should except Prince Edward Island, where they have been asking for extensions. speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: This is a new section to provide that pounds may he established in which lobsters caught during the open season may be placed and sold during the close season. Under the existing law it is illegal to be in possession of lobsters during the close season. This clause worked detrimentally to the interests of our fishermen, and as our close season occurs at a time when lobsters would bring a very high price on the American market, the American fishermen, having no close season, enjoy a great advantage in that market over the Canadian fishermen. Owners of these pounds may sell lobsters which they have caught during the open season, to American fishermen. This traffic must be surrounded with every precaution to avoid breaches of the law, and only after great hesitation and repeated requests have the department adopted this policy. I hone this policy will commend itself to the favourable consideration of parliament and that by it we can give a further advantage to the lobster fishermen.

But, the feature which presents itself most forcibly to my mind is that there are comparatively few places along our coasts which naturally lend themselves to the purpose which this regulation makes provision for, and that consequently there will be comparatively few people who will be able to avail themselves of the advantages of this amendment to the Act. That means then, in effect, that this particular business will, in different localities, become in the nature of a monopoly. There is, of course, another feature to it, and that is that the American palate is to be satisfied and gratified during the Canadian close season, while the poor Canadian will not be permitted to gratify his appetite, and he, as I understood the minister, will have to forego his dish of lobsters, during some months in the year. If the minister does not propose to make any relaxation with regard to the regulation in that respect it would not be lawful for a person operating a pound to sell these lobsters in the Cana-adian market during the close season, as he is only permitted to sell for use out-, side of Canada. The minister, during the discussion which we had some days ago on the subject of the lobster fishery, stated that it was possible for Americans and Canadians to fish for lobsters during the Canadian close season, outside of the three mile limit along the Canadian coast, and sell them in the American market, although they could not at the same time sell them in the Canadian market. It would seem to me that when we admit that that condition is possible, and when we erect these pounds along the coast, whether there be many or few, these two things working together will lend themselves to the violation of the law. The minister knows that there is a very pressing need for the enforcement of a close season, and that with-

out the enforcement of a close season the lobster fishery, if it does not cease to exist, will certainly decline seriously. Indeed, there are many people who think that under existing circumstances the lobster fishery will become depleted, and be a thing of the past before very long. But, it seems to me that there are two dangerous features in connection with this matter. One is that it is bound to create a monopoly in different localities because of the very great expense to which it will be necessary to go to provide these pounds, make them satisfactory, make them safe, make them so that the lobsters can be kept in a healthy and wholesome condition; the other is that where you have these lobsters taken in the open season available to he put in the pounds by the person who is operating or controlling it, you are open to the risk of having lobsters taken outside of the three mile limit, or inside of the three mile limit in all probability, during the close season, and put into that pound surreptitiously. So that, there are these two features which are going to be evident in the operation of this Act when it goes into effect.
I should think that it would be very wise on the part of the minister to have some information, definite and satisfactory, as to the probable cost of the construction of these pounds, and of their maintenance, because, if any person makes application to the department, as I understand it, and that application has the approval of the fishery officer of the department, I take it that the department would be, under ordinary circumstances, in dutv bound to issue a license. speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Jameson) that the fear which he entertains with regard to the possibility of violating the regulations in establishing these pounds has been engaging the very serious consideration of the department for many years, I was telling the committee a few moments ago that years ago we had applications from a number of people asking for the privileges which are now authorized to be given by the legislation under consideration. The department was afraid, as my hon. friend is, that there might be some violation of the regulations, that it would be inciting the people to violate the rules and regulations in the way he has just suggested. However, after giving the matter our most serious consideration, we have come to the conclusion that we should request parliament to give us the necessary authorization to establish these pounds. We will have at each of these pounds a man for the purpose of supervising the operations, and, having an officer in charge of the pound, nothing of an illegal nature can be carried on. There might be some violation, but the man who would do such a thing might incur very serious consequences. The owner of a pound will have to observe the regulations, and if he fails to observe them it is a matter of discretion with us whether we renew his license or not. That will induce him to carry out the regulations properly. In that regard I think that our fears, which appear to have been shared by my hon. friend also, will disappear, and that Ave may expect very good results from this policy. My hon. friend says that this is going to create a menopoly. I do not see how it . can create a monopoly because we will issue licenses to every one who applies. I am informed that the cost of Mr. Baker's pound was $3,800, and I should think that the income

to the owner of the pound will be sufficient to give a fair return for the money invested.
I understand that Mr. Baker's was almost a natural pond, and that the outlay was comparatively speaking small.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I have no doubt that in many cases the cost would be greater.
I understand that it cost Mr. Baker more than the sum mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Mr. Baker stated to the department that it cost him between $3,800 and $3,900. The idea is to sell these lobsters on the American market as well as on the Canadian market, and no lobster' will be allowed out of the pound during the close season except on the certificate of the fishery officer. With all these precautions I should think that the law will not be violated and that a new source of revenue will be opened up to our people.
Is there any size limit on the lobster taken?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No. Berried lobsters will not be permitted to be sold.

The small lobsters are now used in the canneries and when the canneries are not in operation they may be put on the Canadian market out of season, which I think is very undesirable. If you put a size limit on the lobster when placed in the pound it would not be so bad.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I do not think there is any danger that these small lobsters will be sold as fresh live lobsters. Some years ago, as my hon. friend knows, we' abolished the size limit regulation.

Coming from a fishing section of the country I wish to say that I heartily endorse this legislation. For a number of years, in my county there has been a great demand for the establishment of private lobster pounds, the idea being that when the' lobsters grow in the pound to a large size they will be sold at a much higher price than if sold when taken first from the water. I believe that the license fee provided for in the Bill is none too high. In my section of the country there are places, small and large, where if cheap dams are constructed the lobsters can be held, and there fed and cared for. The size limit in Charlotte county waters is 101 inches, and no lobster can be taken out of our waters and sold unless it is 101 inches long or 4f carapace measurement. Those who establish these pounds buy live lobsters from the fishermen, and they cannot buy them undersize in our waters. I am Mr. BRODEUR
sorry to say though that they can bring smaller sized lobsters from the waters of Nova .Scotia, and they can keep these fish in the pounds and feed them until they grow to a larger size. The result is that often the growth of the lobster is from 150 to 300 per cent in say two years and by letting them grow to this larger size they get a much higher price for them in the American market. It pays those who own the pounds to keep the lobsters in them, and it pays the fishermen to sell to the pound keepers, and I cannot see how it in any way injures the lobster fishery. The lessees of the pounds have to take their chances on the lobster dying before growing to the increased size. Therefore, as all the risk is put upon the man who obtains the licenses for pounds, as the government is contributing nothing, and as the fishermen are benefited, I feel that the action of the government in this matter is highly commendable. I heartily approve of this measure as I believe it to be beneficial, judging from my own experience in the waters of my county and from what the fishermen have told me.
How long would the hon. member (Mr. Todd) expect these lobsters to be retained in the pound in order to grow to a marketable size?

Possibly the fishermen who put them in the pound would not care to keep them more than a year. I know of one case in Charlotte county waters where they have been kept for about two years. I may say that I have had a letter from one of the lessees of a large pound which comprises about sixty acres and he claims that his company has already lost about ten thousand dollars in lobsters, but a large part of that loss was due to losing eighty or ninety thousand lobsters in one season, not because, m death or lack of care, but because they got out over the sea wall. The objection to using such a large body of water for a pounH is that they have to use the traps in catching these lobsters as they do in the open sea. In the smaller places little dams could be built so that the water can be lowered, and the lobsters caught in' the open season, and the fishermen are not put to the expense and labour of setting traps. .

May I ask my hon friend what the system is in his county with regard to the storage of lobsters; whether the individual fisherman takes them there and puts them in the custody of the person who ' controls the pound, whether they are taken account of, and accounted for at the end of tjie season or when they wish to remove them, or whether they are sold to the operator of the pound at the time they are taken there.

The fishermen take these lobsters as near the pound as possible, and the licensee then sizes them and pays so much apiece f'or them. When these 150,000 or 175,000 lobsters were brought from these particular waters, I know, from the lobster canners of my own county, that they were complaining because they had to pay a cent a pound more for them than they did before it was found that the owners of these pounds were buying our lobsters and paying a higher price.
The proprietor of the pound takes the risk?
Takes all the risk.

I am glad to know, from what the minister says, that the Canadian epicure is also to have an opportunity of getting an occasional lobster during our close season. I understood, when he first explained the purpose of this amendment, that it was the intention only to allow lobsters taken during the close season to be exported. The minister states that an officer will be placed at each one of these pounds to see that there is no infraction of the law. I do not know whether that will entail the employment of additional officers, but I presume that it will. I have this to say with regard to the officers, and I think it will be endorsed by every hon. member of this House who knows anything about the lobster fishery, that the officers whom the minister may appoint for this purpose will have to be a little sharper and keener and more attentive to their duties than the officers who are at present supposedly looking after the lobster fishery. I think there has been very little attempt on the part of the outside officers of the department to protect the lobster industry, and, whether the minister appoints new officers or instructs the present officers to watch these pounds, I hope they will be given to understand that they are to watch them and see that the law is carried out; because I know that at the present time many of the officers of the department are winking at open violations of the law-the taking of lobsters in the close season and the taking of small lobsters at a time when there was a legal size limit. I hope the minister will give these officers to understand that they are to live up to the letter and the spirit of the regulations, because that is the only way in which the lobster fishery can be preserved. This amendment is opening the door to infractions of the law during the close season, and it is only by a rigid enforcement of the regulations that infractions of the law in that regard can be prevented, and the protection of the lobster fishery can be maintained.
The minister says that a license will be granted to any person making application
for it. I would like him to inform the committee whether there will be any standard of pound, because I can very well apprehend that there may be individuals who, without having any proper place available for the construction of a suitable pound, men perhaps with the best of intentions, but lacking experience in this matter, may make application, thinking they may be able to carry out the impounding of lobsters in a satisfactory way. The minister may remember that two years ago, when the committee sat to take evidence with respect to the lobstery fishery, and particularly with regard to the impounding of lobsters, one of the witnesses, who knew considerable about the matter, declared that there should be certain standard regulations in regard to these pounds, because the sunlight impinging on the backs of these fish when the water over them was not sufficiently deep to protect them, brought about a sickness which made them unfit for human food or killed them outright. So I presume it will be necessary to fix some standard or have some regulation as to where these lobsters may be impounded, and that it will be on the certificate of some officer in that regard that the license will be issued. I would like the minister to inform the committee as to whether the license will as a matter of fact be granted only after an examination by some officer of the department, and when the department is satisfied that there is a proper pound available, in the possession of, or under the control of the person making the application for the license.
