Bill (No. 79) to regulate the manufacture, storage and importation of explosives- Mr. Templeman-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 2,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
I desire to amend subsection (g) in this respect. That section reqds:
'Magazine' means and includes any building, storehouse, structure or place in which any explosive is kept or stored.
The provincial authorities have pointed out that possibly we might be infringing on provincial magazines licensed by the provinces, and after consultation with the provincial authorities we agreed to this amendment:
That after the word 'stored,' the following words be added: 'Other than at or in or for the use of a mine or quarry in a province for which provision is made by the law of the said province.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
As this amendment is made in deference to a suggestion that some portion of the Bill might be an infringement of provincial rights, I should like to point out that this measure save in so far as it deals with the importation of explosives, is clearly something not within the legislative competency of this parliament. This Bill purposes to regulate the way people shall handle explosives, and that has nothing to do with any general regulation of trade or commerce. It undertakes to regulate how any man in his own factory shall handle and deal with explosives and its purpose is the protection of life. It does not seem to me to be anything but a purely local matter in each province, and if you cannot justify it on the ground that it is a regulation of trade and commerce, as the words ' trade and commerce ' have been interpreted by the highest authorities-that is, the regulation of some general nature 'or affecting commercial interchange either between the different provinces or between the provinces and the outside world-I entirely fail to see how you can justify it at all. There is at least one section that makes quite clear how purely local this matter is. I refer to section 10 :
10. No license shall be granted for any factory or magazine hereafter established within the limits of, or within one mile of the limits of any city, town or incorporated village, or elsewhere except with the approval of the municipal corporation or other local authority having jurisdiction, and also with the consent of the minister.
That provision-in itself a most excellent provision-clearly indicates the purely local nature of this legislation. Methods of handling explosives which a man has stored may be perfectly safe in one locality and very dangerous in another; and here you are endeavouring to regulate the handling of explosives by one general law made applicable all over the country. And, because you are seeking to make the law applicable all over the country, I suppose it is inferred that that gives jurisdiction. I would respectfully suggest for the consideration of the minister that that is an unfounded idea. What determines the jurisdiction is the subject matter that is dealt with; and I should certainly be very much interested to know under which of the provisions of section 91 of the British North America Act the minister says he has power to declare how I shall handle explosives in my possession in the particular locality in which I live. So far as this is a licensing Act- for I believe there are provisions requiring licenses-it does seem to me that the provinces certainly would have power to license persons handling explosives. I know that in my own province people have
. 8453

to take out a license for the sale of gunpowder. I think the minister ought to he in a position to point out to us where he finds jurisdiction in this parliament to regulate how people shall carry on their business on their own premises in the locality in which they live. I must confess that, even after some reflection, I have not been able to find the grounds on which this is brought within the jurisdiction of this parliament. I do not say that there are no provisions of the Bill that are within our jurisdiction. The regulation of importation is clearly within -the power of this parliament. And there -may be other provisions also. But the bulk of the sections seem to me to contain provision to secure purely local ends-to secure people from dangers that may Tesult from the fact that somebody is handling explosives in the course of his business or otherwise in these localities.	'

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I would not care to debate the constitutionality of this Bill with my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty). This is a Bill, as he sees, regulating the manufacture, importation and storage of explosives. The Bill was framed by Captain Des-blorough, the chief director of explosives of Great Britain, who came to this country last summer, spent several months examining the conditions of our powder establishments and presented to my department a full report which has been printed and sent to each member. The Bill was subsequently referred to the Department of Justice. I have conferred with Mr. New-combe the Deputy Minister of Justice on the point of the power of -this parliament to legislate on the manufacture of explosives and the regulation of magazines, and I was advised that there was no doubt that the Bill was constitutional. Great care has been taken in the preparation of the Bill not to trench in any way upon provincial jurisdiction.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Under what- clause of the British North America Act does the minister claim jurisdiction? Was it under ' Trade and Commerce '?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
Yes, I think he quoted that as one of the clauses that gave this parliament supreme power. I should like to point out that this Bill is the outcome of a strong public demand. The first request we had for legislation by the Dominion parliament on this subject came from the Ontario Department of Mines. It appears to be impossible for any province to control by regulation the manufacture of explosives and to inspect the explosives to ascertain that they were ot proper composition and not too easily exploded. There ought to be uniformity in the character of the explosives used if the very numerous 267J	.
accidents, such as we have had in the last twelve months, are to be obviated. After a conference with the manufacturers of explosives in Canada, the contents of this Bill were approved of. The provincial governments were consulted, and we had the very able assistance of Air. Thomas Gibson, the Deputy Commissioner of Alines for Ontario. AVe exempt from the jurisdiction of this Bill magazines licensed by a province which has inspectors and the machinery for inspecting magazines. Thus this Bill is really introduced at the urgent demand of several of the provinces, and all the manufacturers and a general public demand. Such catastrophes as have occurred at Sand Point cannot possibly be prevented by any provincial legislation; at least every province would have to pass legislation regulating the character of manufacturing establishments, and would also have to establish an elaborate scientific staff to examine every explosive placed upon the market. The provinces have desired this government to deal with this matter so as to have uniformity.
I would not attempt to argue the constitutionality of some of the Bill's provisions with learned lawyers; I simply state that the Bill has had the endctrsation of the Justice Department. It is highly in the public interest if we can avoid such terrible catastrophes as have occurred. The Hull disaster of a year ago is an example. Four tons of virite exploded-The day before the explosion there were 24 tons in the storehouse near Hull, and if the explosion had taken place while the entire quantity was there I am told the foundations of this building would have been shaken, and the walls might have tumbled down. It is a very serious matter. Even if there is a little doubt as to our power to license powder magazines, there is no chance of objection by any province on the ground that we are infringing on their rights, it is not a question that- the provinces will be too anxious to assert their right to legislate upon.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
The anxiety of the provinces to maintain their rights is the smallest consideration. Just because this legislation is of the greatest importance, and because satisfactory legislation for the protection of the public against danger resulting from explosions is highly desirable, these are the very reasons that make it essential we should have effective legislation. If we have not jurisdiction this will not be effective legislation, and it will make no difference if the provinces do ask for it. If the provinces lie back and do not pass the requisite legislation, when the public good requires it, and leave the matter to us, and we have nothing to justify ourselves except that the public good re

quires such 'legislation, that fact will not make our legislation any more effective, and the result will be that we will have legislation which if it were effective would be most desirable but, if ineffective, would be quite useless and our intervention in the matter will simply serve to lull the people whose duty it is to attend to these things, into the idea that they are being attended to. It is precisely because of the great importance of this legislation that it should be effectively made. I have the very highest respect for the opinion of the Justice Department, and of the Deputy Minister of Justice particularly, and I do not want to criticise it, but it would be a certain satisfaction to us, who have some doubts on this subject, if we could be informed upon what provision in law the Deputy Minister of Justice based his opinion. In the very first section we have a provision that no person shall have an explosive in his possession without a license from the minister. _ If this provision is based upon the jurisdiction of this parliament to deal with the regulation of trade and commerce, I fail to see how this House can impose upon me the necessity of having a license from. f)h!e minister in order to have an explosive in my possession. That surely has no connection with trade and commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that that is unless it is an authorized explosive.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I am within the provisions of this law if I have it in my possession without any idea of dealing with it in any way. The provisions with regard to selling explosives are open precisely to the same objections. I have great respect for those who have asked for and recommended this legislation and for the provincial authorities, but ail of these things constitute no answer to the question that may be raised as to the effectiveness of this legislation. The answer to the objection which will be made will have to be found in the British North America Act, and I think that certainly it is regrettable that we are not to be put in a position to know just in virtue of what power we are taking it upon ourselves to make this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: It may be a little late to rectify an error after the legislation that it is endeavoured to enforce is found to be unworkable. If you are relying on this legislation, when perhaps the jurisdiction is not here to prevent the great evil of the uncontrolled handling of explosives, you are running the serious risk of meeting a. situation where you have nothing but the fancied security resulting from illegally enacted legislation. While I do not propose to press the point too far, still it is one which deserves serious consideration, and if the Department of Justice, have given it serious consideration, I suppose they have said the last word on the subject. At all events, I shall be able to feel that I can sleep soundly and that I have no further responsibility in the matter.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
I think that the minister must be a disciple of the late Oliver Mowat. He said at one time that when-

ever there was a question as to the right of the legislature to legislate upon any subject although he was fully satisfied that it had such a right, still he went on the assumption that it had, went on and legislated and left it to the courts and the people afterwards to determine whether the legislature had or had not that right. He was not very much concerned whether he had authority so long as he honestly believed he had and he went on and legislated.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: And he enacted a lot of good legislation.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
If the minister gives the ordinary meaning to the words ' kept and stored ' I believe that this legislation will go farther . than is contemplated by him. As I read the Bill it would prevent the sale or storage of any cartridges, or percussion caps in any ordinary store in any town in Canada. Let me read clause (g) of section 2:
_ 'Magazine5 means and includes any building, storehouse, structure or place in whioh any explosive i6 kept or stored.
Section 6 says:
The minister may issue licenses for factories and magazines, and no one shall manufacture, either wholly or in part, or store explosives except in licensed factories and magazines.
Clause 10 provides that:
No license shall be granted for any factory or magazine hereafter established within the limits of, or within one mile of the limits of, any city, town or incorporated village, or elsewhere except with the approval of the municipal corporation or other local authority having jurisdiction, and also with the consent of the minister.
If we take this language in the ordinary way I think it will prevent the sale of ammunition by any hardware store in Canada.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: How is it that the province takes that right to itself? It is only during the last session of the legislature of Ontario that a law was passed prohibiting the sale of firearms, cartridges and such things for the peace and safety of the people. This legislation deals with explosives and firearms. The province must believe that it has the right to do so in the interests of the peace and safety of the people. We are dealing in explosives as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
A great deal of this Act will be put into force by regulation. We will act on the advice of experts. Section 18, paragraph (e) provides that:
The Governor in Council may make regulations for excepting from the operation, of this
Act shops, stores and other places where small quantities of explosives are kept for use or sale.
There is no desire to interfere with the sale of explosives in stores. My hon. friend refers to the word ' magazine5 in the interpretation clause. Of course, powder and cartridge in a country store, or in a city store for that matter, would noi. be in a magazine to be licensed by this Act.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The Bill says that * magazine ' means any place in which any explosive is kept or stored. I do not see where any exception is made.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I think that the minister's explanation that he is going to do by regulation what he could not do by law is rather a strange assumption of legal power.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Well, it is absolutely neces'sary to make proper regulations in this case.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
Shall.the proposed amendment to subsection (g) be carried-that at the close of subclause (g) the following words he added:
'Other than at or in and for the use of a mine or quarry in a province by which provision is made by the law of such province for the efficient inspection of mines and quarries.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
Mr. TEMPLEMAN moved that the following be inserted as a new clause after clause 2:
This Act 6hall not apply to the Department of Militia and Defence or to the Department of the Naval Service.
The Department of Militia and Defence secure their ammunition under proper supervision, and they do not want any interference by the Department of Mines.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Is the Department of Militia and Defence allowed to manufacture and keep unauthorized?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: But this Act does not apply to them. Some of the provisions of this Act are framed to prevent injury to certain people living near the manufac-turies and storehouses and it would be in teresting to know if the Department of Militia is to be allowed to keep storehouses in places dangerous to the people in the neighbourhood. Can the minister say that an explosive belonging to the government would not have the same dire results as an explosive manufactured by private individuals? So far as the Department of Militia is concerned, there is no authorized explosive, because this Act does not apply * to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The Department of Militia and Defence U3es English explosives and all English explosives have for years come under a similar provision. There is no explosive sold in England that, is not tested and that has not been authorized. The Militia Department uses proper explosives under proper conditions.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The minister has not answered the question put by the hon. member for Parry Sound, as to whether it was the intent of the Act to prohibit the sale of ordinary gunpowder in the regular hardware stores?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Unquestionably and undoubtedly it is not the intention to prohibit or interfere with the sale of powder in stores except it be that we have machinery, in this Act for the inspection and testing of explosives, and there will be no unauthorized explosives allowed to be sold anywhere. This Act will not interfere with their keeping small quantities authorized explosives in an outhouse, or a store, or anywhere else.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The interpretation clause says that an explosive means among other things, fireworks, fuses, rockets, percussion caps, cartridges, and ammunition of all kinds, and clause 6 says that the minister may issue licenses for factories and magazines and no one shall manufacture or store explosives except in licensed factories or magazines. The Act certainly would seem to contemplate the prohibition of the sale of powders by small stores. How can the minister reconcile these provisions of the Act, what do they mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: They mean exactly what they say. All that the Bill will have to do with these things is to provide as to the care and safety of the chemical combinations in them. If the Act is not clear that it does not apply to the storage of small quantities of ammunition, gunpowder and so forth by the retail trade or the wholesale trade for that matter, I am quite willing that it should be made clear. The word magazine3 applies primarily to magazines in connection with manufacturing establishments for the storage of very large quantities of explosives. I read in the papers recently a good deal about a magazine on the Montreal road, within a few hundred yards of a considerable population, where explosives are stored in very large quantities. It is magazines of that kind that this Bill purposes to deal with, and I am quite willing to make it so clear that there wdll be no reason to interfere with small quantities of explosives kept for sale in stores.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
Would the minister be willing to have a separate section reading in this way:
Nothing in this Act shall apply to shops, stores or other places where small quantities of authorized explosives are kept for use or sale.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The minister has just explained that 'magaizne,' in his interpretation, means a large magazine for storing large quantities in connection with the manufacture of explosives. But the question is not what his interpretation is if the Bill becomes law. The Bill purports to make the explanation, and it says that 'magazine'- means and includes any building, storehouse, structure or place in which any explosive is kept or stored. That is very clear. The Bill also siays what an explosive is, and it includes in that term caps, ordinary ammunition and fireworks; so that ordinary ammunition could not ibe kept in any store or in any room without a license. I may say that I am not objecting to the Bill, because I think the principle of it is a good one.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Will the minister define what a small quantity is?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I suppose such quantities as merchants keep.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: A wholesale merchant might keep several tons, while a retail merchant might keep very little.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: We might strike out 'small quantities' and say 'shops or stores where explosives are kept for use or sale.'

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The amendment apparently entirely destroys the definition of a magazine as set forth in section 2, or at all events restricts it to places where explosives are kept neither for sale nor for use. It would appear to me that a place where a man kept explosives neither for sale nor for use would be a very restricted number of places. The manufacturer who keeps his explosives in a magazine is keeping them for sale at some period, and this amendment would make the Act utterly inapplicable, no matter how large the quantity was, unless it were kept for sale or use. It seems to me that the amendment is absolutely contradictory of the definition cf a magazine in the Bill.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Why not define the word ' magazine ' as including any building in which any explosive is kept or stored except retail stores where explosives are kept for sale, and private houses where explosives are kept for the use of the owner thereof.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
Better let that clause stand.
On section 3,
3. Except as herein provided, no person shall have in his poseession, or import, store, use or manufacture, whether wholly or in part, or sell, any explosive unless such explosive has -been declared by the minister to be an authorized explosive.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: We have had to-day a Bill which provides that no one shall go into the salmon canning business without a license. We have on the statutes an Act providing that no one shall go into the whale fishing business without a license. We know that a monopoly was given to one company for the whole whale fishing business. It seems to me we are carrying on this license business a .little too far. It is not always easy to get these licenses. There is no prescribed course whereby anybody who wants a license can come to the government and easily get it. It takes a long time, and in a great many instances the license is refused. And sometimes, when friends of the administration find out that other people are applying for the licenses, they come in and the first applicant" does not get the license but the friends of the government do.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: What kind of a license?

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Any kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Name one.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I could- name one if I chose.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: This is a very good time to do it.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
I have one case in mind where that fact exactly happened. I would suggest that -this matter should be safeguarded in some other way. It seems to me it could be safeguarded by having regulation and inspection with a heavy penalty for violation of the regulations. This matter is of very great importance to the province from which I come. In reading the report of Captain Desborough, and the suggestions he made,.it occurs to me that this Bill is going to very materially increase the manufacture of explosives, and so increase the cost to the consumer. The Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) is well aware that the cost of powder is a very serious expense particularly in British Columbia where powder is used so extensively both in the mines and in the clearing of land. While I am not prepared to say that precaution should not be taken for due care and the prevention of explosion, yet, I submit that very great care should be taken that the cost of production is not unduly increased. Captain Desborough, I
understand, is an expert in charge of the military powder manufactories in England.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Director of explosives.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: At any rate he is connected with the imperial army, is he not?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: He is an officer on the retired list, but belongs to the Home Office. He is enforcing the Explosive Act.,

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: At any rate, he is a government official, and the factories he is familiar with

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: No, he has charge of the inspection of all the manufactories in England.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: At any rate, there can be no doubt that in a closely populated country like England greater precautions are required so far as storing explosives is concerned than in a country like this. In a country of that kind they are more likely to go into more expensive work and operation 'than is necessary in a sparsely settled country. Therefore, I -would suggest to the minister that he should be very careful to see to it that the recommendations of Captain Desborough do not unduly increase the cost of production. It is .curious-I do not say that there is any connection between the two facts-but I am informed that just at the time Captain Desborough came here in connection with this manufacture of explosives, a company was formed in England with a capital of $10,000,000 with the idea of making a merger of several large powder companies throughout the Dominion of Canada. And it is obvious, that while there may ,be, as I say-and I do not suggest that there is any connectionbetween the two facts-but it would be obvious that the more expensive the manufacture of explosives is made, the less danger there is of competition against a trust of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: There is no limitation to the number of licenses to be issued. Any person can go into the manufacture of explosives. I have no fear that because we are going to issue licenses and to regulate this business, we shall increase the cost. As a matter of fact, the English explosives are selling for less than others, and they are manufactured under careful regulation. There will be no limitation of the number of manufactories. Under the Department of Inland Revenue there is no limitation of the number of distilleries. You can all have licenses for the manufacture of alcohol if you like, and the same wall be true with regard to this other kind of explosives.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
The point I was trying to make is that if the cost of production is increased-as, undoubtedly, it must be- that would have the effect of deterring other

people from going into the manufacture. If I read aright the recommendation and report of Captain Desborough, he stated that in manufacturing they put too many machines of one kind in one building, also that too large a quantity of explosives was stored in one building, also that there should he embankments of earth between the different buildings-and generally made a number of recommendations which meant undoubtedly very largely increased cost of manufacture. The manufacture of giant powder and gunpowder, I understand, is a comparatively simple and cheap matter. But if you are going to hedge it about with restrictions of the kind I have indicated, you are going to increase the cost of production and the cost to the consumer. That would make it necessary to have more capital in order to start in the business and would certainly keep others out of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: My hon. friend, I trust, does not wish to continue the present conditions. The conditions of manufacture have been condemned by Capt. Desborough, and the changes are all designed to avoid accidents. In my hon. friend's own country there were two or three disastrous accidents last year. I do not know the cause of those accidents and it is to deal with these questions that this Bill is introduced. As to the increase of cost to the manufacturer a representative of every manufacturer, especially in Eastern Canada, conferred with Capt. Desborough and heartily supported the provisions of the Bill. They are all prepared to continue manufacturing under the conditions of this Bill.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend did not think I objected because the cost to the manufacturer would be increased? Capt. Desborough states that they were not going to disturb to any extent existing plants, and I object to the minister saying I am not in favour of the principle of the Bill. I have not the slightest objection to every attempt being made to safeguard the lives of those engaged in this industry, but we must be careful not to so increase the cost of production as to make the purchase of powder any greater burden than it already is in British Columbia.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: What is meant by an authorized explosive and how is the declaration that an explosive is authorized to be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: When an explosive has passed the tests prescribed under the supervision of the inspector of explosives, and is approved by him, the minister will declare it an authorized explosive. The chemical composition will be the basic principle of the test.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I sympathize with the object of the Bill in regard to protecting the lives of those engaged in the manufacture of explosives, and also those who use them; with the largely increasing use of explosives in our various industries, it is essential to have an Act of this nature, so that any criticism I have to make is not because I am opposed to the principle of the Bill. It seems to me that the Bill will interfere with certain provincial rights, and will bring about confusion and conflict where the province has effective legislation. If the Bill was confined to the manufacture of explosives and their use for specific purposes, and did not embrace the sale and stronger of all kinds of explosives, some of these difficulties might be overcome. Has the minister consulted the various provinces to avoid conflict with provincial Acts? Once the Dominion parliament legislates, that legislation will override any provincial Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The hon. member for St. Anne Division (Mr. Doherty) raised the question of provincial rights, but he has thrown responsibility for the constitutionality of this Bill upon the government, and is not pressing that point. As far as the constitutionality of the Bill is concerned, I am resting entirely upon the' opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice. The Bill was referred to all the provinces, and they were all satisfied with it and were very anxious that a general law for all Canada should be passed by the Dominion parliament.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I did not have the opportunity of hearing all the discussion on this Biil, but the remarks that the hon. member made have attracted my attention to the possibility of a conflict of jurisdiction which might arise. In my province we have very complete regulations as to the use of explosives in connection -with the mines, and these laws have been found to work very satisfactorily. I trust that the minister has made provision in the Bill, which I regret I have not studied closely, to see that there is no infringement with these regulations as they are already provided, particularly in the mines. _ Where you have to deal with the coal mining industry, where the lessees and operators of these mines, hold under the Crown, and where the Crown, represented by the_ government of a particular province, introduces regulations into the leases under which they hold and operate these mines, I think it would not be wise for the federal government to interfere.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
The Bill does not touch the use of explosives at all either in a quarry, or in railway construction, or in a coal mine. All it aims at doing is to

secure the manufacture of as safe an explosive as possible. We purpose putting on the market only authorized explosives.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Much of what is contemplated by this Bill is done already by municipal by-law under provincial authority. The legislative assembly has given power to the municipalities to pass bylaws regulating this same thing. Therefore, it must toe in conflict with provincial legislation and provincial rights to that extent. The minister said, in reference to some observations toy my hon. friend from Montreal St. Anne (Mr. Doherty), that we are not making a law to cover this condition, tout that we are making regulations to cover it. It is done by regulation. Power to make regulations is under the statute law, and if the statute law is unconstitutional the regulations can certainly have no force or effect. When we are confronted with such an uncertainty as this the government have it in their power to provide a means whereby they can be satisfied. They can make a stated case, send it to the Supreme Court and have the verdict of the court whether this law is wholly constitutional or only partly constitutional. What has the minister to say about that? I think we should have some reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
I do not agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) at all that we ought to make a stated case. I do not know what stated case we could make or how to bring the case before the Supreme Court. There is no doubt in the minds of my officers that this parliament has power to regulate the manufacture and importation of explosives and the whole purpose of this Bill is to regulate the manufacture, storage and importation of explosives. We believe we have that power, but if we have not that power we will soon find it out when the law is put in force. I think that the best way to get a decision as_ to the constitutionality of a law of this kind is to put it in force, because we will find out much more quickly in that way than by taking a stated case to the court.
I do not think we are wrong and I do not know that I can say any more to my hon. friend than I have already said, that I am acting on advice with regard to the constitutionality of the Bill, and therefore, I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman that we should drop this Bill and have a stated case. It might take two or three years to get a decision on that point. As a matter of fact, this Bill was intended to be introduced last year, and we have been somewhat criticised for dilatoriness in not having brought it forward sooner. In the meantime there have been two or three most disastrous explosions the fatal results of which might have been avoided if a Bill
of this kind had been upon the statute-books.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: It is true that the minister says he has been fortified by the advice of the Justice Department, but this is not the first time that we have found the Justice Department wrong on constitutional questions which have been decided by the Supreme Court. I admit that while the favourable opinion of the Justice Department is a strong justification for legislation along that line when it is clear that there will be a conflict of authority, I think it is ample justification for submitting a stated case to the Supreme Court. The minister says that it would be two or three years before we would be likely to get a verdict. Does he mean to say that the Supreme Court is so impotent and indifferent that it would take two or three years to get a decision from that court? They might decide the case at the first sitting of the court, and consequently it could not be more than six months before the case was decided. I think it would be much better to avoid improper legislation if it can be avoided by stating a case for submission to the Supreme Court than to pass legislation and then afterwards find that a great deal of litigation might result from it, and that we are obliged to go back and abandon what we have done as being unconstitutional or ultra vires.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: It will be regrettable if the question of jurisdiction results in failure to safeguard the lives of those engaged in the handling of these dangerous explosives. This is not a new question. It has been before the public for some years and it is recognized that something should be done to safeguard human life. This Bill, as my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) points out, only deals with the manufacture of dynamite.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: It goes further than that.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
It aims at preventing the continual sacrifice of human life by explosions. In the last three years 114 lives were lost from premature explosions on railway construction work in this country. The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Barnard), a few minutes ago, expressed the fear that this legislation might increase the cost of manufacturing explosives. It seems to me that all Canadians should agree that human life should be of more consideration than dollars. The greatest cost that this country has paid for explosives has been the cost of human life. I hope my hon. friends will not press this question of jurisdiction, but will allow the Bill to go through and see if something cannot be* done to safeguard the lives of those who

are compelled to handle these dangerous explosives.
On section 4,

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Thi3 is a class of legislation, of which we have had a good deal this session, by which we hand over blindly our legislative power with regard to a particular matter, to the Governor in Council. We say here that no man should have a right to do different things except as permitted by the regulations which are to be made under this Act, and the Governor in Council is empowered to make any regulation he chooses and to impose any conditions whatever upon the permission to be given. When the power of legislation was confided to parliament it was with the idea that parliament should use it and not hand it over blindly to be used by the executive government of the country. I quite understand that there may be details that are better dealt with by regulation than by statutory enactment, but when we simply say that no person should have the right to do the things mentioned here unless he gets permission in accordance with such regulations as the government may make, it seems to me we are going too far in the direction of delegation. The minister must have some idea in his own mind as to what the conditions are on which this permission should be granted and he should put in this Act some definition of what these conditions are, so that we may have even a general idea of what we are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I can send my hon. friend the English Act, and there he will see that the regulations are very voluminous and very technical and highly scientific. This Act could not be administered in any other way than under such regulations.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: How would this section affect chemists who are constantly experimenting with these explosives?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
Permission would be given for keeping a small quantity.
On section 6,

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The municipalities by by-law specify that merchants may keep these explosives in segregated buildings. Would not this section interfere with the municipal authority in that respect?

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The issuing of license pertains to the province, and I do not think the federal government has any power to issue them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: We will let that stand.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: On section 7,

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: This clause is open to the same objections that I made to the Bill in the first place. The provisions and definitions in this Bill would make it impossible for any man to bring into Canada a box of cartridges, percussion caps, or fireworks. I do not think it is the intention of the minister to prohibit the importation of cartridges either from Great Britain ot the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Of course, the intention is to prohibit the importation of explosives that are not authorized. There is no explosive imported from Great Britain that is not authorized.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The clause reads, importation of authorized explosives. Under this clause a man would require to have a permit from this government before he could cross the line with a box of cart? ridges. Is that the intention of the minister? The people dealing in these goods which come from Great Britain would have to get a permit from the minister for every shipment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: There is not much use of our testing and inspecting explosives manufactured in Canada, and not permitting any except those authorized to be sold, if we are going to permit explosives that are not authorized to come from another country. All the explosives from Great Britain are authorized, and of course they will be admitted.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Do I understand that the intention is to permit the importation only of those explosives authorized by the government and those authorized by Great Britain? Is it the intention to prohibit the importation of explosives from the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I am advised that in the United States the government is proceeding along similar lines and has in connection with its geological survey a testing station for explosives, and is now authorizing explosives. Explosives authorized in that way by the United States government would probably be approved of without any further examination by our testing officers. But explosives which are not tested or authorized by the United States government would have to be tested by our testing stations before they could be passed.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
I do not think the minister understands the objections I am raising. It is simply this. There are a large number of American rifles brought into this country by parties coming in the hunting season. They import cartridges

for these rifles, and under this clause they would have to get a permit each time they imported these cartridges, whether authorized or not.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I think the minister does not perhaps understand the situation. Last season, in the hunting season, a number of hunters had purchased a certain kind of Remington rifle, which took a certain kind of ammunition. Within five or six days of the opening of the season those who. endeavoured to secure cartridges for that rifle discovered that they could not obtain them from the hardware stores, and small retail stores and had to wire to the makers in the United States to secure that kind of cartridge. If a case of this kind arose under this Act, the small retailer would have to go to the trouble of getting a permit from the government, which would make it impossible for him to secure these cartridges at the time of the hunting season. I think an exception should be made there. I would like also to ask what is ' the manner authorized by the Railway Act' for transportation of explosives. We all know that the railways are authorized under the Railway Act to transmit ammunition or powder of any kind. If I remember rightly, a terrible explosion occurred on one of the railways at Stratford, in western Ontario. If this Act is to be of any use, I think these regulations should apply directly under this Act, and should not have any reference to the Railway Act. I would like to know if the minister knows what the regulations under the Railway Act are.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I confess I am not very familiar with the regulations, which occupy 25 pages. As the transportation of explosives is provided for by the Railway Commission under the Railway Act, we exempt it in this Bill.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
Suppose these regulations of the Railway Act were transgressed by a railway company, and trouble arose,_ and a suit was brought, what authorization has the Railway Commission under the statute to make these regulations? The most dangerous thing in connection with explosives is the handling of them on the railways, and I think this Act should be made to apply to railways. For instance, a railway is carrying in the summer time dynamite that was made in the United States. It has saw-dust filler. When the warm weather comes the nitroglycerine -will thaw out of the saw-dust filler and will leak through the box to the bottom of the car. If a drop of that happens to go on the railway track, there is an explosion and the car goes up in the air. That is what happened at Stratford. If this Act is to be of any use, it should
be made to apply to cases like that. I would like to know if the Railway Commission has any power to make these regulations, and if they have the force of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The Railway Commission, in adopting these regulations, say that under the powers and in pursuance of sections 26, 230, 286 and 287 of the Railway Act, the board approved of these regulations.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Do these regulations limit the carriage to authorized explosives?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: This does not refer to authorized explosives.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Why not have a reference made to those regulations of this Act, 'and have them authorized under this Act?

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Why not let this clause stand and have a reference making those regulations legal under this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: These regulations are legal now. They have been passed by the Railway Commission under the Railway Act.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Small arms and ammunitions should be excepted and there should be no necessity for a permit in their case.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I think that the objection with reference to small arms is valid. The minister seems to be under the impression that unauthorized explosives can be taken into the country without permit. If he will read the section he will find out that permits may issue for the importation of authorized explosives and the unauthorized cannot be brought in at all. A man who tries to bring in 100 rounds of 22 cartridge in his valise or a dozen firecrackers will be liable to a penalty unless he gets a permit. A great number of 'hunters, come from the United 'States to Ontario and Quebec, and they bring their ammunition. They should not be liable under section 7.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: But explosives under this Bill are meant explosives in large quantities. Under clause 18 the Governor in Council may make regulations, and he has ample power to exempt small arms and ammunition from the operation of this Bill.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
Take the two provinces of Quebec and British Columbia, which are largely advertising their game, that is becoming quite an asset of both provinces. They are coming, as the minister knows, all the way from Europe. I was given the 1 names of several who have come on two or

three occasions from Germany with a party and who have spent considerable sums of money in order to engage in hunting the large _ game of British Columbia. I only mention that to indicate the importance of this section, for under this section, when these men arrive, any game warden or any body else can stop them on the border and hold up all their arms and ammunition, and before they can bring a single particle oi ammunition in it will be necessary for them to get permission from the government here at Ottawa. I think it would be well that that question should be looked into, because it comes up in so many clauses of the Bill, and a proper section drawn, to cover the point, so that the Bill may be made effective. I think the minister admit-in fact it is not discussable at . at this is the effect of the section, r \ ?s no* a 'mere objection for the sake of objection from hon. gentlemen on this side, but it is an important question. And, unless the Bill is amended it would lead to considerable trouble, especially as I have already pointed out in these two provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I quite agree that ammunition for small arms especially, should be exempted from the operation of the Bill, otherwise it would lead to very considerable confusion. I would assume as a matter of fact-I am only giving this as an opinion-that all ammunition used in small arms should be of the best kind and certainly good enough to be authorized.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: But, even if authorized it would be necessary to get a permit. That is the difficulty. There should be some way of exempting ammunition for this purpose. I think it would be well for the minister to let this section stand, and draft a section that would cover that point.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: It would seem that the Bill contemplates that, because 'safety cartridges ' are defined in the interpretation clause. In making new regulations all you would require would be to provide that, safety cartridges may be exempt.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
Shall section 7 stand?
On section 8-special permits,

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: It does not say to whom this special permit is to he issued. I should think an analyst would be the only one person who would require it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
This provides that for purposes of analysis and scientific research a quantity not exceeding two pounds may be imported. The Bill gives permission to anybody to submit an explosive for analysis. Scientific men may want to investigate, and, on payment of a small fee, Mr. GOODEVE.
they may be permitted to import in quantities not exceeding two pounds.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
For chemical analysis two pounds is more than enough.
On section 9-applicants for licenses to furnish plans of factory and premises.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: What authority has the minister to issue licenses? As I understand that under the law the power to grant a license to carry on business remains entirely with the provincial parliament. The law will permit the Dominion government to allow a person to carry on a business, or to prevent him carrying it on. But I do not think it will permit the department to license anybody. If the minister will consult the legal department of the government, I think he will find that he cannot give licenses. That has been tried by this parliament on several occasions, and I understand that the decision has been against it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: We discussed that point at considerable length before the hon. member (Mr. Currie, Simcoe) came into the House. I said I would abide by the opinion of the Justice Department that this is a power we have a right to take-the powep to license for the purpose of regulating the manufacture.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Subsection (a) provides that the plan is to be drawn to a scale, and is to include ' also all the lands adjacent thereto on which buildings are erected.'. I understand by lands adjacent thereto the lands of adjoining owners. I would think there would be some limitation on the word ' adjacent.' It might be mistaken to mean ten miles or half a mile.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
That is the meaning. Of course the interpretation would depend on the configuration of the land. A factory might be placed quite close to a building if there was a small mountain or hill between, possibly within 100 yards, while in a very flat district it might have to be a mile away. I see no reason to specify the distance more closely.
On section 10, factories not to be built near towns, &e.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Why is the distance of one mile from an incorporated village, &c., stipulated. Are there statistics to show within what distance from a city a factory [DOT]would be safe?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: This is copied from the English regulation. They have statistics there, and I presume one mile has been found sufficient. The explosion at Hull was not more than a mile from where we are standing.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The minister is mistaken; it is nearly a mile and a half from here to Eddy's factory.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
I think I would move to have that read two miles. As we are giving authority to establish factories without the consent of a municipality, we should make it two miles unless with the consent of the municipality.
Mr. iSPKOULE. The distance which would be safe must depend largely on the amount of explosives kept.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
I would move to insert after the word ' jurisdiction ' in the 39th line, the words:
Or the government of the province in any province and in a territory where there is no local authority having jurisdiction, and also with the consent of the minister.
That is to meet the view of the government of Ontario.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Does the amended section mean that a factory cannot be established within a mile of a city, town, &c., even with the consent of the municipality, that it can only be established a mile away with the consent and that within a mile it cannot be established under any condition?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The clause means that it shall not be nearer than one mile.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Within a mile there cannot be a factory?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: No. [DOT]

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: And more than a mile away they must have the permission of the municipal authority and the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: That is my understanding.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Let us understand how that would affect the situation. Hardware stores that sell gunpowder and blasting powder, store it in a building.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: We have allowed one clause to stand for the purpose of meeting that point.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: But that was with regard to ammunition.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Quite true, but we propose to narrow the interpretation so as not to include stores.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
Yes, for otherwise you are in direct conflict with the provincia1 authorities, because they provide where explosives may be stored, and you may give authority with Tegard to handling and storing them in a way which under the provincial Act, could not be done.
On section 10:	Consent of municipality
and minister before license granted.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: It is suggested that even although a municipality might give consent a mile is very close. It might be necessary to have a two mile limit. Take the city of Ottawa; an outside municipality might give consent to have a factory within a mile although the city would not care to have a large factory of that kind within a mile, and so I think we had better make it ' within two miles.'

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: I do not want to make the conditions too onerous. If the conditions under which the explosive will be required to be manufactured are lived up to, and if by close inspection the danger is minimized, and the quantities of explosives to be kept in buildings are also minimized to the lowest possible extent, the conditions as to the configuration of the ground and the proximity of other buildings being taken into consideration, I would think a mile not too close. I desire to be on the safe side and, on the other hand, I do not want to make conditions that would be too onerous to the manufacturer. I will be guided 'by the House in that respect," but I think that one mile should stand in the section.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
I can conceive from what the minister says that it might be a hardship to force a factory to go more than one mile from a village. It says:
Within one mile of the limits of any city, town or incorporated village.
But, it would make a great difference, if it were close to a large city where the damage and loss of life might be much greater. In a small municipality there would not 'be the same danger as where there were crowded buildings, and a large population. It might read ' witnin two miles of 'the limits of any city, or within one mile of the limits of any town or incorporated village.'

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
I would rather not change it.
i Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe). There are sev-' *eral cities which are fortified and there are magazines in the fortifications which are used by the dealers of explosives in those cities. How would you work it there?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: If the magazines are used by the Militia Department it would have no application.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The magazines of the Militia Department are used by the trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
Then the Bill would operate.
On section 11: Permits for experiments, and testing new explosives.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: A man might be experimenting with a new explosive. Many are doing that in the hope of getting something newer and (better than anything on the market.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: But that is covered in both places.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: No, clause 4 provides far chemical iexperiment and (the making of explosive for scientific purposes, not for practical use. Section 11 authorizes the minister to issue a permit for manufacture for experimental purposes. An inventor thinks he has a new idea and he wants to experiment in the manufacture of an explosive. It may be permitted by this clause.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Clause 4 would allow a man to make small quantities of explosives for experimental purposes in his laboratory. He could endeavour to discover a new kind of explosive. In clause 11 you say that if he has paid the fees prescribed by regulation he can manufacture for experimental purposes. I cannot see how these two clauses can work together.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
They might work together right enough, but one is for the making of a small quantity of explosive, for chemical experiment, and the other is for the testing or manufacturing of blasting powders or explosives for special blasting operations only. The section says that the minister:
May issue a permit to manufacture for experimental purposes or for testing and special blasting operations only, and not for sale.
They are two different permits.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Is there any difference between ' making*' and ' manufacturing? '

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Not much difference.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: Not very much difference. In the one case a man could not make a large quantity of the explosive. It does not limit him as to whether he shall conduct original research or whether he is following in the footsteps of some other experimenter and developing the quality of an explosive which he might not have discovered or made.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: The object of giving that permission is to allow people to experiment with blasting powder and the producing of a new powder. They must have that permission or they would be prohibited from doing that without a license.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext: If you retain section 4 I do not see any necessity for section 11. Under section 4 a chemist oan manufacture a small quantity of this explosive in his laboratory, but if he proceeds to test it he will come under the penalties provided in section 11.

maintopic: REGULATION OF THE MANUFACTURE OF EXPLOSIVES.
speechtext:
I think it is about time we should adjourn. There is no hope of our being able to get through this Bill to-night.	.
Progress reported.
